consolidate-release-indexer-and-rollback-manifest-generator-for-private-installer

Introduce a single release indexer and rollback manifest generator for the private-installer packaging pipeline.

Motivation: current release metadata for private deployments is fragmented across per-arch Helm indexes, tarball lists, and ad-hoc rollback blobs which complicates automated upgrades and makes rollbacks error-prone.

This PR adds a deterministic release-index.json format that aggregates artifacts (helm charts, installer tarballs, OCI blobs), provenance pointers (cosign signatures, sbom hashes, attestation references) and a compact rollback-manifests/ directory with incremental patches used by the installer to perform atomic rollbacks.

Changes: - add cmd/release-indexer: builds release-index.json from CI artifacts, computes deterministic stable IDs, attaches provenance bundle references, and emits signed index + incremental patch files - add cmd/rollback-gen: produces rollback-manifests/<release>-<seq>.json that the installer uses to roll back a specific component set - update private-installer Helm chart values and templates to read release-index.json and prefer pinned artifact URLs when present - terraform/modules/s3-buckets: add new prefixing and lifecycle policy used to host both indexes and incremental patches - CI: new workflow .github/workflows/release-indexer.yml that runs indexer on build artifacts, cosigns the index, generates SBOM deltas, and publishes to release-buckets - docs: document index schema, upgrade flow, and rollback semantics - tests: unit tests for stable ID generation, e2e test that simulates an upgrade then verifies rollback-manifests apply cleanly Notes on implementation: the indexer computes stable IDs using a canonical JSON serialization and sha256 over (artifact URL, arch, variant, semantic version, builder-provenance).

The rollback-gen ensures patches are idempotent by using a three-way diff against the previous index and emitting reverse-apply steps.

Security: cosign signing and sigstore attestations are integrated in CI; the installer verifies signatures and rejects unsigned indexes unless an explicit permissive flag is enabled.

Backwards compatibility: indexer emits a legacy-compatible shim for older installer releases that still read per-chart indexes.

Migration plan: CI will publish both legacy files and the new index for two release cycles; a follow-up PR will flip the installer default to prefer the index.

See linked Linear ENG-3482 for rollout milestones.

tooling/execution: concurrency safeguards and tool-result-injection ergonomics

Motivation: Customers integrating complex tool chains reported flaky outputs when multiple tools ran in parallel and tool results were injected back into the model stream.

This PR standardizes execution semantics for multi-tool calls, adds runtime safeguards for parallelism, and harmonizes behavior with our OpenAI-compat surface.

Summary of changes: 1) Executor: introduce a per-request "tool-parallelism" cap (configurable at API/route level) that bounds concurrent tool invocations and provides backpressure hooks to the scheduler; 2) Injection protocol: formalize a deterministic injection ordering when multiple tool results arrive within the same model turn and attach an idempotency token to each injected result so retries do not duplicate content; 3) Retry semantics: new retry policy enum (none, best-effort, strict-idempotent) exposed via the API and respected by the runtime and OpenAI-compat shim; 4) Streaming stability: when streaming responses include tool-calls, we now atomically flush tool-invocation markers to the stream and gracefully resume generation once injected results are committed to the KV cache; 5) OpenAI-compat updates: function-calling payloads now accept an optional "execution_hints" map with parallelism and idempotency hints that the compat layer translates into our internal routing and executor options; 6) Observability: emit new metrics (tool.invocations.active, tool.invocations.queued, tool.injection.latency) and traces annotated with execution_hints for easier debugging.

Implementation notes: - Executor changes are confined to runtime/executor/* and api/handlers/tool_call_handler.go; the executor preserves the previous scheduling algorithm but applies per-request parallelism caps before dispatching tool workers. - Injection order uses a deterministic comparator: (request_tool_sequence, tool_priority, start_timestamp).

This avoids nondeterministic interleaving in model-visible outputs. - Idempotency tokens are short-lived UUIDs persisted in the request context and kept in the per-request token-cache; replayed tool results with matching token are ignored by the injection layer. - The OpenAI compatibility shim accepts additional fields but falls back to previous behavior when execution_hints are omitted to preserve backward compatibility.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc updated with sequence diagrams and failure modes (ENG-1523) - [x] Unit tests for ordering and idempotency - [x] Integration tests simulating multi-tool fan-out and parallel retries - [x] Metrics/tracing added and tested in canary - [x] Backwards compatibility verified for existing function-calling clients - [x] Docs snippet for API surface added Notes on tradeoffs: We intentionally chose a conservative default parallelism cap of 4 to reduce burst load on downstream tool services; customers can raise this per-route with a warning in the console.

The idempotency token approach requires minimal state but does not protect against cross-request duplicate side-effects (we call this out in the design doc).

Migration: No action required from existing users; new execution_hints fields are additive.

For customers wanting deterministic injection ordering across retries, they should include explicit tool priority in their tool manifest.

Rollout plan: Canary on a small percentage of hosted traffic for one week with annotated traces and enhanced logging; force-enable flag included to accelerate rollouts for enterprise tenants.

Backwards compatibility: tests included to ensure older SDKs (OpenAI-compat) do not break.

Risk and mitigations: The biggest risk is increased latency when a tool result arrives slightly after generation — mitigated by configurable timeouts and an async-fallback policy that allows the generator to continue with a best-effort placeholder if strict-idempotent is not set.

Local testing: see integration test harness in tests/integration/tool_invoke_fanout_test.go.

jurisdictional-sink-orchestrator: idempotent reconciler + terraform module hooks for private installs

Motivation: Private installations running in multi-region VPCs need deterministic, auditable wiring of audit-log export sinks per jurisdiction and a reconciler that is safe to re-run during installer upgrades and rollbacks. Current behaviour relied on imperative hooks in the installer which caused drift when upgrades failed mid-flight and made it difficult to guarantee retention policies in cross-region setups. This PR introduces a jurisdiction-aware sink orchestration controller and wiring hooks for the private installer + Terraform modules so audit sinks are created and reconciled idempotently.

Summary of changes: 1) Add a small long-running reconciler (go controller) that watches AuditSink CRs and desired sink mapping from the installer; it performs create/update/delete with strong idempotency guarantees and emits detailed audit events (sink-reconciler.* metrics). 2) Extend terraform modules with new outputs and lifecycle-driven hooks so the private-installer can emit a desired-state manifest into the cluster (terraform/modules/audit_sink/*). 3) Helm chart changes: templates now include jurisdiction labels, retention annotations, and optional lifecycle hooks to defer reconciliation until KMS/secret rotation completes. 4) Installer: on the private-installer side we add a declarative sink-write step that applies the desired-state manifest and waits for the reconciler to report success; this replaces the previous ad-hoc shell provisioning. 5) Tests and e2e: add deterministic e2e that simulates mid-upgrade failures and validates rollback idempotency and retention enforcement.

Checklist: - [x] Controller implemented with retries and backoff, idempotent create/update path - [x] Terraform module hooks and docs added - [x] Helm templates updated for jurisdiction and retention annotations - [x] Installer wiring uses desired-state manifest for reconciliation - [x] Unit + e2e tests added and passing - [x] tfsec and helm linting addressed (one warning suppressed with justification)

Deployment notes: - This is backward compatible: the reconciler will adopt existing sinks by matching labels, so rollout can be done with a simple Canary (deploy reconciler -> enable terraform desired-state output -> flip installer to use manifest). - For air-gapped installs the reconciler image is included in the private registry bundle; ensure registry credentials are present prior to enabling the controller. - KMS-backed sinks: reconciler respects annotated kms_key_ref and will wait for secret readiness before finalizing sink wiring.

Rollback behavior: the reconciler is intentionally conservative: on deletion it removes only sink resources it created or owns (ownerReferences + managed-by label). If an installer rollback is triggered mid-upgrade, re-running the installer applies the same desired-state manifest and the reconciler converges back to the prior state without orphaning temporary resources.

Related work and references: Linear tickets ENG-2147 and ENG-2153 track the reconciler and terraform integrations. See internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/board/ENG-2147/jurisdictional-sink-orchestration and runbook: docs/private/audit-sink-orchestrator.md

Why this is different from previous PRs: previous changes focused on retention lifecycles and sink rotation; this change focuses on making sink wiring declarative and upgrade/rollback safe at the installer and terraform boundaries so compliance operators can guarantee retention and export topology after any control-plane operation.

dsid_00cba40e229f454fb7f1722b446d93ff__p.text: Improve stream teardown, retry/backoff and reconnect semantics for OpenAI-compatible streaming

Improve stream teardown, retry/backoff and reconnect semantics for OpenAI-compatible streaming

Fixes a class of customer-facing streaming failures observed when clients disconnect mid-stream and then reconnect or retry. This PR centralizes stream teardown logic, adds an explicit session idempotency token for resume/reconnect, implements server-side exponential backoff for automatic retry attempts, and updates the OpenAI-compatibility adapter to preserve in-flight function/tool-call state across reconnects. Key goals: 1) avoid duplicate function/tool calls on client reconnect, 2) ensure server timeouts produce a deterministic terminal event that client SDKs can use for cleanup, 3) make streaming retries safe under load without amplifying downstream work. This is implemented as a small runtime change plus adapter and SDK patches and includes unit+integration tests and a controlled rollout plan. Migration notes: server behavior is backward-compatible for clients that don't use resume tokens; SDKs should be updated to take advantage of resume and idempotency tokens to prevent duplicate tool calls. Rollout: staged on Dedicated for 48h, monitor stream-error-rate and duplicate-tool-call metrics, then full rollout to hosted API.
Maya Patel: Can we guarantee no duplicate tool invocations if the client retries while the server is still performing the call? Please add a test that simulates a long-running tool and a mid-call reconnect.
Author (Jinsoo): Added reconnect_test.go that simulates a long tool and asserts single invocation; we also added a server-side in-progress marker to prevent dupes.
Carlos Nguyen: The backoff defaults look conservative; suggest 100ms base, 2x multiplier, 1s max for hosted. Also, add metrics for retry_attempts to make rollout observable.
Author: Applied suggested defaults and exported retry_attempts metric; documented in console alert playbook.
Ethan Brooks: OpenAI adapter event naming changed from 'done' to 'complete' in one place; keep both for 2 releases for compatibility.
Author: Kept legacy 'done' event emission and added 'complete' alias with deprecation note in docs.
Stable streaming: deterministic teardown on disconnects; resume tokens to reconnect without duplicate tool/function calls; server-side retry/backoff to avoid thundering retries; OpenAI adapter preserves function call state across reconnects; SDK updates available for smoother migration.
Clients that want deduplicated reconnects should upgrade SDKs to the patched release and use the resume token exposed on stream start. Existing clients continue to work but will not benefit from resume semantics. Monitor metrics: streaming.duplicate_tool_calls and streaming.retry_attempts during rollout.

ci: generate release graph and manifest validator for private-installer artifacts

Motivation: CI for private installer releases lacked a machine-readable release graph and a manifest-level validator that ties signed artifacts (images, helm charts, tf modules) back to the release manifest.

This PR adds a release-graph generator and a manifest-validator stage to the private-installer CI pipeline to ensure provenance, enable safer upgrades/rollbacks, and block unsigned/unaligned manifests from publishing.

Summary of changes: - new pipeline step 'build:release-graph' which produces a directed release graph (JSON) that maps artifacts -> helm chart values -> terraform module versions and includes cryptographic digests and SBOM references; graph is collated from build outputs and attestation metadata - new pipeline step 'validate:manifest' that consumes a release graph and enforces: cosign signature verification (keyless and KMS), SBOM presence, chart values checksum, and compatibility matrix checks for upgrades - small helper library under tools/release-graph that normalizes artifact metadata, computes canonical digests, and emits signatures-ready metadata for the signer job - Helm chart linting rules extended to emit a Helm manifest fingerprint (stable ordering) and surface mismatches between chart contents and release graph - Terraform module manifest extraction to include provider pins and a short policy check to prevent unsupported provider upgrades in the same release - CI orchestration changes: the validate step runs before artifact promotion and blocks publishing to the release bucket on failure - added an automated delta-rollback manifest generator which creates a minimal rollback plan from the release graph when a canary fails Why this is different: existing pipelines stamp artifacts and upload indexes, but we need a top-level release graph that can be consumed by Private control-plane for deterministic rollouts and by on-prem installers to reconcile manifests during upgrades.

This PR focuses on making the release artifact a first-class, verifiable graph rather than loose indexes.

Checklist: - [x] release-graph generator implemented - [x] manifest validator implemented and integrated into the CI workflow - [x] cosign verification (keyless and KMS) wired into validator - [x] Helm fingerprinting integrated - [x] Terraform module extraction implemented - [x] unit tests for tools/release-graph - [x] e2e run in staging that simulates signed artifact promotion - [x] added docs for ops on how to interpret the release graph Changes included (high level): tools/release-graph/* (new library and CLI), ci/pipeline/build-release-graph.yaml (new job), ci/pipeline/validate-manifest.yaml (new job), charts/private-installer/patches/manifest-fingerprint.yaml (helper), terraform/modules/release-metadata/README.md (docs), scripts/delta-rollback/gen-rollback.sh (new helper), tests/integration/release-graph-e2e (e2e harness).

Testing and verification: - unit coverage for release-graph normalization functions - integration test that generates a release graph from staged artifacts, signs them with a test KMS key, then runs validator (CI job uses real cosign verification in staging) - staging rollout run that exercised the delta-rollback generator after a simulated canary failure - CI history shows two failed validator runs during early iteration (missing SBOMs) which were fixed by the chart/lint rule update Rollout plan: - merged to main and enabled in staging for one week; manual gating for production release (ops approval required) - enable automatic blocking on validator failures for subsequent releases; until then validator failures are opt-in via release-note flag Migration notes: - existing release index consumers must be updated to prefer release-graph.json; a small compatibility shim is provided under tools/release-graph/bin/compatify - operators must ensure cosign public key or KMS access is available in the Private control-plane to verify signatures Security considerations: - cosign key usage requires KMS scopes; the validator supports both keyless (OIDC) verification and KMS-backed verification; by default validator rejects unsigned artifacts - SBOM presence is mandatory for private installer releases; policy can be relaxed via a per-customer policy file if needed Documentation: - docs/private-installer/release-graph.md added explaining format and how to use the delta-rollback generator - ops playbook updated with steps to manually validate a release graph Known limitations & follow-ups: - release-graph currently serializes all digests in SHA256; we will add multi-algo support (ENG-6780 follow-up) - we do not yet have an automated remediation when validator fails (ENG-6723 will track a retry/auto-fix job) Related: ENG-6723 (release graph spec), ENG-6780 (multi-algo hashing), SUP-3048 (support ticket where customer asked for deterministic rollback plans).

Add deferred-indexing RAG playbook and streaming tool-proxy adapter

Summary: Adds a compact RAG playbook that demonstrates deferred (background) indexing semantics combined with a streaming tool-proxy adapter for tool-calls.

Motivation: many production RAG pipelines need to accept writes (ingestion) while keeping the serving index stable; fully reindexing synchronously is expensive and causes visible latency spikes.

This playbook shows a pragmatic pattern: 1) ingest -> enqueue -> optimistic-serve from a hot prefix cache; 2) background indexer that performs incremental merges and emits cleanup/metrics; 3) a streaming tool-proxy that forwards tool calls to external services via a websocket-backed relay and exposes a local replay hook for offline tests.

What this PR contains:
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/README.md: conceptual notes, sequence diagrams (ASCII) and runbook for tradeoffs.
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/docker-compose.yml: minimal local stack (producer, indexer, redis queue, preview server).
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/examples/ingest_client.py: small Python client that demonstrates optimistic reads and enqueue semantics.
- adapters/tool-proxy/streaming-relay.ts: TypeScript websocket relay and proxy adapter used by the playbook.
- adapters/tool-proxy/README.md: integration notes for connecting external tools (auth patterns, backpressure).
- docs/snippets/deferred-indexing.md: docs site snippet with recommended config flags for Redwood Optimize (batch/kv-cache hints).
- tests/integration/deferred_index_smoke.test.ts: basic e2e smoke tests for local run.
- examples/workflows/deferred-index-github-actions.yml: simple GH action to exercise the local smoke test.

Notable behaviors and examples:
- The playbook intentionally demonstrates an 'optimistic serve' where new documents are queryable from a short-lived prefix cache before a full index merge completes; this is annotated with caveats in the README.
- The streaming-relay supports an ACK/receipt flow and a fallback HTTP webhook mode for environments without websockets.
- docs/snippets/deferred-indexing.md includes recommended Redwood API routing policy snippets to route low-latency reads to cached shards while background merges are underway.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc and sequence diagrams included
- [x] Local stack + smoke tests
- [x] Adapter with replay hooks for testing
- [x] Docs snippet for console and Optimize guidance
- [x] Basic perf notes (cost/latency tradeoffs)
How to run locally (short):
1) git clone && cd playbooks/deferred-indexing
2) docker compose up --build
3) python examples/ingest_client.py --sample
4) open http://localhost:8080/preview to see optimistic reads
5) run npm run test:smoke from repo root to execute the integration smoke test
Implementation notes and tradeoffs:
- Background index merges intentionally batch writes with a small window (500ms default) to minimize merge amplification; the README explains tuning knobs for batch size and TTL.
- The optimistic prefix cache is TTL-based and uses sequence numbers to avoid serving uncommitted partial writes; we document consistency tradeoffs and recommended SLOs.
- The streaming tool-proxy was implemented in TypeScript to mirror many frontend integrators; a Python minimal shim is left as an exercise in the README.

Security: the adapter includes an optional HMAC handshake for websocket relay auth; README outlines how to replace with KMS-signed tokens in Private deployments.

Migration and docs site: the docs snippet adds a new sidebar entry under "Authoring -> Playbooks" and references Redwood Optimize recommendations (batching, kv-cache sizing) so that customers can reproduce the topology.

Introduce batch-pattern compiler and compact quant telemetry

Motivation: Tenant workloads show recurring micro-patterns that are not well captured by the existing static batch templates.

This PR adds a batch-pattern compiler that consumes recent request traces and emits compact, tenant-scoped batching templates plus a paired compact quantization profile telemetry pipeline so the Optimize layer can recommend lower-cost model variants without losing quality.

Scope: 1) batch-pattern compiler service (server component and CLI to compile patterns from trace snapshots); 2) compact quant telemetry exporter that aggregates per-pattern token distributions and per-model quantization sensitivity metrics; 3) lightweight simulation harness used by CI to validate unit economics vs baseline; 4) minimal Console integration: a read-only API endpoint surfaces the top-3 generated patterns for a tenant.

Implementation notes: the compiler is conservative by default (max batch-size delta +/− 20%) and emits safe fallbacks.

The telemetry export uses a compact protobuf envelope and ships via the existing telemetry pipeline with optional batching disabled for immediate visibility.

Rollout plan: staged deploy to canary tenant group -> 48h metrics observe window -> ramp to 20% -> full.

Includes feature flag redwood.features.batch_pattern_compiler and a tenant opt-in tag.

unify-credential-modes-and-peekable-stream-iterator-cross-sdk-ergonomic-bump

Introduce CredentialMode enum across Python/TS/Go SDKs, add a peekable streaming iterator to improve ergonomic consumption of chunked responses, harmonize retry/backoff presets, and bump SDK package versions to align with the new session APIs.

Context: Multiple SDK consumers requested clearer credential behaviors and a simpler streaming consumer pattern.

This PR introduces a small, explicit CredentialMode enum (AUTO|PINNED|DELEGATED) across the Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs, harmonizes default retry/backoff presets to match runtime SLOs, and adds a peekable stream iterator abstraction to make chunk-aware consumers easier to write.

Motivation: reduce accidental double-refreshes, improve cross-lang parity for session lifecycle, and reduce user code complexity when implementing lookahead on streaming responses.

Summary of changes: - Add CredentialMode contract and adapter in core session layer (sdks/*/session) - Implement CredentialMode-aware credential provider fallback chain with telemetry hooks - Add PeekableStreamIterator (py: IterablePeek, ts: PeekableAsyncIterator, go: PeekableChan) with small memory bounds and deterministic close semantics - Align retry presets and expose an ergonomic RetryProfile builder for advanced use - Add compatibility shim for Node backpressure (ts) preventing unbounded in-memory buffering - Update docs and migration notes and bump package versions (py 2.8.0, ts 1.16.0, go v0.10.0) Checklist: [x] unit tests for credential modes and adapter chains [x] integration tests for stream iterator under chunked responses [x] e2e smoke on hosted API against a Canary model [x] docs: cross-sdk migration guide and examples [x] changelog entries Impact: API surface additions are additive (new enum, new iterator helper).

introduce-guided-sprint-quickstart-with-local-probe-and-telemetry

Motivation: provide a compact, opinionated RAG quickstart that teams can run locally to iterate on retrieval, prompt steps, and lightweight telemetry. The Guided Sprint quickstart is intentionally small: it demonstrates a stepwise RAG pattern (index -> retrieval -> refine -> tool call) with deterministic seeds and a local probe harness for reproducible smoke tests and telemetry sampling. This PR adds the quickstart scaffold, a tiny local probe that simulates user flows and emits simple structured telemetry, and a short doc snippet for the dev docs site.

What changed (summary): added quickstarts/guided-sprint/README.md with step-by-step setup, added a sprint.yml authoring manifest describing step contracts and assertion hooks, added probe/local_probe.py which runs deterministic sessions and records JSON traces to /tmp/guided-sprint-traces, added examples/simple-agent.ts showing how to wire Redwood SDK tool-calls and structured output checks, added docs/snippets/guided-sprint-embed.md with docsite copy and a short inline gallery, and added ci/quickstart-smoke.yml to run the local probe in CI smoke.

Checklist: - [x] Quickstart scaffold and README - [x] Deterministic probe with seed control - [x] Telemetry lightweight JSON trace format documented - [x] CI smoke job that runs probe (non-blocking, optional rerun) - [x] Inline doc snippet for docs site - [x] Tests: basic smoke assertions in probe

How to run locally: 1) python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate 2) pip install -r quickstarts/guided-sprint/requirements.txt 3) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=<key> 4) python quickstarts/guided-sprint/probe/local_probe.py --seed 42 --count 10 5) Inspect JSON traces at /tmp/guided-sprint-traces and run quickstarts/guided-sprint/validate_traces.py for basic assertions.

Telemetry and expectations: traces are intentionally minimal: each step emits {"step": "retrieve|refine|tool", "lat_ms": <int>, "tokens": <int>, "status": "ok|warn|fail"} and an overall session summary. The README documents how to plug the traces into Console by uploading the JSON or using the small adapter script included.

Compatibility: the example agent uses the public Redwood SDK patterns (prompts -> structured JSON -> tool calling) but avoids any private APIs. The quickstart is suitable for hosted and local flow testing; it does not assume Dedicated or Private deployment.

airgap-minimal-shrinkwrap-and-almalinux-support-with-registry-replication-module

Motivation: support customers that must run private/on-prem installs on RHEL derivatives after CentOS8 EOL and enable much smaller, curated airgap bundles that operators can generate for minimum-viable installs.

This PR adds AlmaLinux 8/9 node support to the installer images and packer build pipelines, introduces a 'shrinkwrap' bundle manifest and generator that produces component-level minimal bundles for air-gapped installs, and provides a Terraform module to replicate selected container images into a local registry (with optional Content Trust and signed manifests).

The Helm chart changes add an initPreload hook template to load images into local registries before startup and a TLS-pinning option for registries with self-signed certs.

Operational improvements: preflight checks for kernel modules and container runtimes were extended for AlmaLinux variants, and we add an atomic rollback script + helm rollback wrapper that replays saved release manifests from delta bundle metadata.

Backwards compatibility: old full-bundle installer remains the default; shrinkwrap is opt-in via `bundle-profile=shrinkwrap` and has a documented schema.

Includes docs and examples for generating a shrinkwrap bundle, configuring registry replication, and an e2e smoke test for an AlmaLinux VM in an air-gapped network.

Interleaved activation checkpointing and buffer coalescing to cut peak GPU workspace

Motivation: In production we observed recurring OOMs and large transient workspace peaks for long-sequence (>=4k) generation and KV-heavy batched workloads. Previous work focused on per-layer checkpointing and arena sizing; this PR targets three complementary levers to reduce peak GPU footprint without changing numeric behavior: 1) interleaved activation checkpointing that staggers recompute windows to shrink concurrent activation sets, 2) scratch buffer coalescing that merges short-lived per-op scratch allocations into a reusable sub-arena, and 3) scheduler hints that adjust continuous-batching flush thresholds to avoid pathological peak overlaps with KV cache refill phases.

Summary of changes (commits):
- commit 1: implement interleaved checkpoint planner and unit tests (planner/ckpt_planner.{cpp,h}, tests/ckpt_planner_tests.cpp)
- commit 2: introduce coalesced scratch allocator and sub-arena lifecycle (runtime/scratch_coalesce.{cpp,h}, runtime/sub_arena.{cpp,h})
- commit 3: hook allocator into kernel queue; add allocator metrics and tracing points (runtime/kernel_queue.cpp, observability/metrics_registry.cpp)
- commit 4: scheduler hint API and continuous-batching adjustments (scheduler/flush_policy.{cpp,h}, api/scheduler_config.md)
- commit 5: perf harness & benchmarks (perf/bench_long_seq.py, perf/bench_report_24678.md)
- commit 6: address review comments, test flakiness fixes, additional microbenchmarks (various)

Files/areas changed (high level):
- runtime/*: new scratch coalescing allocator, sub-arena management, updated kernel queue to use sub-arena
- planner/*: new interleaved checkpoint planner for grouped layers
- scheduler/*: new flush threshold heuristics and opt-in scheduler_hint config
- tests/*: unit tests for planner and allocator, end-to-end perf harness
- perf/*: benchmark scripts and result artifacts
- docs/api: scheduler config doc and short rationale

Key implementation notes:
- Interleaved checkpointing preserves existing deterministic recompute semantics; it schedules which layers are recomputed together to minimize the live activation set. The planner uses a simple greedy grouping heuristic with a max-concurrent-activation target derived from a per-model profile.
- Scratch coalescing introduces a short-lived sub-arena that consolidates fast scratch allocations from kernels that previously carved many small temporary buffers. Sub-arena size is auto-sized from recent epoch allocation histograms and is reclaimed per-batch. The allocator implements a small freelist and uses 8- or 16-byte alignment to avoid fragmentation.
- Scheduler hints are opt-in via the scheduler_config and default to conservative values for existing deployments. When enabled, the scheduler slightly reduces continuous-batching accumulation when the planner predicts a high KV-cache refill overlap (important for chat/history workloads).

Benchmarks (high level):
- Long-sequence generative (seq_len=8192, batch=1): peak GPU memory reduced by 24% (median across 5 runs), workspace allocation spikes reduced by 38%. End-to-end latency unchanged +/- 2%.
- Standard throughput workload (seq_len=2048, batch=4): throughput improved by ~6% due to reduced fragmentation and fewer transient allocations; median latency improved 4%.
- KV-heavy batched chat test: mean memory footprint down 18%; lower variance in tail latency under sustained load.

Compatibility & testing:
- Numeric equivalence tests added for a representative transformer block; recompute paths validated against baseline determinism tests.
- New unit tests cover planner heuristics and allocator corner cases (fragmentation, sub-arena resize). Perf harness includes CI smoke checks; full perf suite runs in infra-perf job.

In our microbenchmarks recompute time increased by <3% while peak memory dropped significantly. Added unit tests and perf samples to perf/bench_report_24678.md to illustrate."

The combination yields both lower peak and lower variance in memory usage for KV/continuous-batch heavy workloads.

Introduce per-turn microtimeline, cost-slab annotator, and alert-playback tool

Motivation: customers often need to correlate per-conversational-turn latency spikes with exact token-cost patterns and the alerts that fired. Existing rollups show per-invocation aggregates but do not surface intra-turn hotspots or let SREs replay alert conditions against synthetic traffic. This PR introduces three complementary pieces: (1) a per-turn microtimeline metric set (lightweight per-token latency and kernel-path tags), (2) a cost-slab annotator service that maps token streams to discrete cost bands for compact storage and alerting, and (3) an alert-playback utility that replays historical traces against new threshold configs to measure alert churn and false-positive risk before changing SLOs.

What this changes: Adds a microtimeline exporter in the runtime that emits compact per-turn sparklines and per-token phase markers; a background annotator that consumes those streams and emits cost_slab labels (low/medium/high/peak) with references to kernel execution path and quantization profile; a new CLI/tooling endpoint in observability-playground that can ingest a time window and run an alert-playback to produce an AP/recall style report for alert configs.

Checklist:
- [x] Runtime: microtimeline exporter (sampling: deterministic 1:50 + priority hotpath overrides)
- [x] Annotator: cost-slab algorithm + deterministic hashing for stable slab ids
- [x] Storage: compact slab label + sparkline rollup schema migration (backfill support included)
- [x] UI: dashboard panels and sparkline widgets (draft)
- [x] Tooling: alert-playback CLI + HTTP endpoint for automated runbooks
- [x] Tests: unit tests for slab binning, end-to-end playback against synthetic traces

Introduce header probing + prefetch bridge for streaming tool-calls and structured-output OpenAI-compat adapter

Motivation: customers reported intermittent failures when using browser-based streaming tool/function-calls behind proxies or CDNs that drop or re-order custom auth headers. The failures manifest as aborted streaming sessions or tool-call rejections during the initial tool metadata exchange. This PR adds a small, backward-compatible probe-and-bridge flow that reduces the likelihood of mid-stream failures and clarifies the header contract for OpenAI-compatible clients.

Design summary: we introduce an OPTIONS-based 'header-probe' that the client MAY issue prior to establishing the streaming WebSocket/HTTP stream. When supported, the probe negotiates which of the following headers will be preserved across the proxy path: X-Redwood-Signed-Nonce, X-Project-Key, X-Org-Scoped-Token. If the probe detects header preservation issues, the client can use the 'prefetch bridge' endpoint (/_prefetch_bridge) which accepts the signed nonce via a short-lived POST and returns a one-time session token tied to the tool-call handshake. The session token is compatible with existing signing semantics and is safe to include in standard Authorization headers and cookie-based proxies.

Compatibility layer: to preserve OpenAI-compatibility we add a structured-output adapter for tool and function call handshakes. The adapter maps legacy header names (openai-internal-* and api-key variations) to our canonical headers, and normalizes nonce/signature frames emitted in stream chunks so older clients and proxies that split text frames do not lose signature context.

What changed (high-level commits):
- add header-probe controller and OPTIONS handler
- add /_prefetch_bridge token issuance handler (short-lived, single-use tokens)
- structured-output adapter for stream frames and legacy headers
- client SDK helper for JS (prefetchBridge helper + probe fallback)
- end-to-end tests simulating proxies that strip headers; unit tests for signature chaining
- docs and migration notes for the compat adapter

Files of note changed: api/http/probe_handler.go, api/http/prefetch_bridge.go, runtime/stream/adapter/structured_adapter.go, sdk/js/prefetch_bridge.ts, docs/auth/header_probe.md, tests/e2e/proxy_strip_headers_test.js, ci/config.yml

Testing and QA: added E2E tests that spin up a lightweight proxy that optionally strips X-* headers and validates the prefetch bridge flow. Manual test plan in docs includes: (1) browser streaming through Cloudflare worker that strips custom headers, (2) server-to-server streaming with preserved headers, (3) tool-call with function metadata larger than 8KB to verify chunked signature frames are re-assembled. Also ran perf microbenchmarks: prefetch bridge adds ~0.7ms median to cold connection establishment but reduces mid-stream abort rate to 0.02% in our proxy simulations.

Rollout plan: feature gated behind 'auth.probe' and 'auth.prefetch_bridge' flags. Default behavior: probe disabled, bridge available. We will enable probe gradually in canary clusters and monitor streaming-success-rate and auth-fallback-count in the first 48 hours. If rollout is clean, we will enable probe by default for SDKs with version gte 1.23.0.

Notes: this PR is intentionally conservative about token lifetime (30s single-use) and logs minimal nonce metadata to avoid PII. See docs/auth/header_probe.md for threat model. Related: ENG-1229 (streaming stability), ENG-1304 (auth header semantics).

Introduce sequence-length-transition-emulator and tail-amplification detector

Motivation: existing synthetic workload runners focus on fixed sequence-length distributions or simple bimodal mixes. Real traffic often exhibits abrupt shifts in token-length distribution (for example, a UI change that causes prompts to include an extra context block) which can amplify tail latency due to cache fragmentation and kernel scheduling. This PR introduces a small, configurable suite that emulates sequence-length transitions and a lightweight detector that flags 'tail amplification' events during benchmark runs.

What this PR adds (high level): 1) seqlen_emulator: a runner that generates workload traces with controlled Markov-style sequence-length transitions (configurable transition matrix, dwell time, burstiness). 2) tail_amplification_detector: streaming detector that computes amplification ratio (p99_after / p99_before) and issues annotated events for the reporting pipeline. 3) integration harness: glue to run the emulator against existing perf-canary clusters and produce JSONL time-series for the reporting pipeline. 4) docs and example profiles.

Checklist: [x] emulator core + config schema, [x] detector + unit tests, [x] integration harness and example Linear job, [x] perf CI workflow that can replay saved traces against baseline, [x] docs.

Why different: unlike sequence-mix synthetic runners this tool models transitions (the temporal dimension of distribution change) and explicitly measures amplification of tail quantiles rather than just absolute p99. This helps identify scenarios where short bursts of longer sequences cause disproportionate cost/latency impact.

Unify session telemetry and introduce compact SDK adapter bridge

Summary: This PR introduces a compact adapter layer across the Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs that standardizes session telemetry envelopes, simplifies the streaming handoff surface, and provides a compatibility bridge so existing consumers can opt into the new ergonomics incrementally.

Motivation: Multiple internal integrations observed inconsistent session envelope shapes, duplicated telemetry keys, and slightly different retry defaults between SDKs leading to confusion for platform teams and noisy alerting.

This was called out in ENG-2143 and tracked as part of cross-SDK parity work in ENG-2199.

Goals: (1) standardize the session telemetry payload and sampling keys across SDKs; (2) provide a minimal adapter that consumers can layer over existing session code to get the new semantics with zero downtime; (3) align retry default presets for streaming and token refresh so cross-language clients have comparable behavior; (4) bump SDK minor versions that contain the ergonomic API surface.

Changes: - Core: new compact adapter module implemented in each SDK repo (redwood-sdk-python, redwood-sdk-typescript, redwood-sdk-go) and exported from the polyglot 'redwood' root package so examples can import a single compatibility shims path. - Telemetry: unified envelope format: {"session_id","span_id","sampling_rate","client_version","env_tags"} and a lightweight sampler hook.

Existing telemetry keys are preserved as aliases for backwards compatibility. - Streaming ergonomics: introduced 'CompactSession.handle' API that wraps existing pullstream/pushstream handles and provides a small set of methods (start, pause, drain, handoff) with clearer lifecycle semantics. - Retry presets: converged streaming retry presets to 'aggressive' (low-latency, limited retries), 'balanced' (default), and 'durable' (longer tail, idempotent workloads).

converge-sdks-backoff-telemetry-ux

Context and motivation: This PR brings a cross-SDK convergence change set across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs to standardize backoff semantics, emit richer retry/streaming telemetry events, and smooth a few ergonomic rough edges in stream consumers.

The goal is parity for default retry behavior (exponential+jitter with an optional max_elapsed config), clearer telemetry for upstream callers to reason about retries and resumptions, and small UX improvements that avoid surprising edge cases observed in recent incidents.

Primary user-facing improvements: (1) unified default backoff parameters and an explicit opts.backoffConfig/BackoffConfig typed object in all SDKs; (2) new telemetry hooks that emit structured retry/stream events (retry_attempt, retry_backoff_ms, stream_resume_token, stream_graceful_fallback) which are lightweight and safe to enable in production; (3) TypeScript: introduce async iterator helper that returns a single unified StreamResult shape and avoids orphaned promise rejections when consumers bail early; (4) Python: contextmanager for streaming responses so that KV cache and network resources are deterministically released; (5) Go: connection pooling opt-in flag and graceful drain on iterator Close to reduce spurious reconnect storms during scale-downs.

Non-goals: changing server-side protocol or adding new server features.

Implementation notes and trade-offs: to keep runtime overhead minimal, telemetry events are emitted through the existing metrics bridge with a new compact schema (no heavy JSON payloads) and a per-client sampling rate controlled by client options.

Backoff defaults were chosen based on analysis of production latency distributions in ENG-3392 and tuned to avoid excess amplification during transient infra blips.

Rollout plan: roll out SDK versions to registries behind feature flags and flip defaults in minor release after a canary week.

atomic release staging, Helm preflight hooks, and compressed release manifests for safer private-installer rollouts

Motivation: private on‑prem/VPC upgrades require greater atomicity and preflight validation to avoid partial rollouts and long rollback windows.

This PR introduces a small release staging layer, Helm preflight hooks (pre-install/pre-upgrade/validate), and a compact compression/packing step for release manifests and provenance files so that the installer can stage an entire release snapshot atomically and validate it before switching the live release pointer.

Design summary: 1) release-stager: an ephemeral staging area in S3/GCS with an atomic 'active' pointer object; publish pipeline uploads a packed, signed archive and a JSON index; after successful post-signature validations the pipeline atomically swaps a symlink-style object (bucket key replace) to make the new release active; 2) manifest packing: index_pack.go creates deterministic tar stream, zstd compresses blobs with level 3 for speed, and the pack includes SHA256 provenance metadata for each entry to simplify verification during installs; 3) Helm preflight hooks: small Helm hooks run before install/upgrade to validate node resources, image accessibility, KMS availability, and required CRDs; failures are surfaced early and abort the Helm transaction; 4) installer/rollback: upgrade tool gains a two-phase apply with an automatic dry-run validation and a deterministic rollback plan derived from the staged index so rollbacks are fast and do not rely on ad-hoc heuristics.

CI changes: new pipeline job ci/pipelines/release-stager.yml validates packing/compression, runs signature verification, and performs a smoke deploy to minikube in under 6 minutes.

Security: signing routine ensures reproducible tar order before cosign signing and inserts a small attestation with build-info and builder git-ref.

Backwards compatibility: published archives include both packed zstd artifact and legacy uncompressed blobs to allow older private-installer clients to continue fetching if necessary; rollout plan includes a two-week dual-read window before deprecating legacy path.

Testing: unit tests for packer and signature validator, integration tests for staged swap and Helm preflight, and manual canary in a staging VPC.

Rollout: merge -> pipeline produces staged artifact -> run canary promotion job -> after 24h and monitoring approval, auto-swap active pointer for production.

See release_notes for more details and migration steps.

Introduce telemetry-gradient and cost shingle inspector for prompt-shape drift detection

Motivation: We see recurring low-signal cost regressions tied to prompt-shape shifts (different prompt lengths / role-token mixes). Existing token-level cost metrics show totals but do not surface subtle distributional drift across segments of the prompt. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) a telemetry-gradient metric that tracks per-invocation changes in token-cost density across prompt segments (head/mid/tail) so we can detect gradual drift; 2) a 'cost shingle inspector' abstraction that slices invocations into fixed-size token shingles, computes lightweight histograms, and emits compact sketches for downstream aggregation and dashboarding.

Goals: - Detect prompt-shape drift earlier without full trace sampling. - Provide actionable panels in the Console to show which prompt segments and model stages (embedding/encode/generate) are driving cost changes. - Add tuned alerts for gradual drift (low-amplitude, long-window) and a higher-sensitivity alert for sudden spike in tail-cost.

Summary of changes: - telemetry/gradient: new metric generator in the observability pipeline. Computes per-invocation gradients between head/mid/tail cost densities and emits incrementally aggregated counters and sketches. - telemetry/shingle: shingle extractor that emits token-shingle sketches (count-min + percentile sketch) keyed by route + prompt-shape-bucket. Light-weight, safe for high QPS. - console/dashboards: new "Prompt Shape Drift" dashboard with:  * Shingle heatmap (fractional cost per shingle)  * Gradient trend lines (head vs tail)  * Attribution panels (by model stage and kernel) - alerts/rotation: new alert rules and suppression windows to avoid noisy alerts for stable seasonal prompts. - tests: unit tests for shingle extractor, integration test harness (synthetic replay) to validate drift detection and alert thresholds.

Backwards compatibility: instrumentation tags are additive; feature can be controlled by runtime flag telemetry.shingle.enabled=false for on-prem.

Rollout plan: - Stage 1: feature flag off in prod; enable for canary tenants (5%) with verbose sampling. - Stage 2: increase to 25% and enable dashboard ingestion. - Stage 3: global rollout with tuned alerting and canary auto-disable if cost overhead exceeds 1.5%.

Related: ENG-3412 (prompt-shape drift pilot), SUP-789 (customer incident that motivated tail cost alerts).

Priya: Shingle key is route + prompt_shape_bucket (3-5 buckets) + stage; we also apply reservoir sampling at 1% by default for high QPS tenants. Maria: Alert thresholds look aggressive for multi-tenant bursts. Suggest adding a rolling baseline with seasonal smoothing. Priya: Added seasonal baseline and a low-sensitivity 'warm' alert group; kept the 'spike' alert high-sensitivity. Samir: Nit: move constants to config and document default cost oversight. Priya: Addressed, moved to helm values and documented. Post-merge: Observability SRE to watch canary and adjust suppression windows on first week.

runtime-validate-response-schemas-and-stream-rewind

Adds a runtime-level JSON Schema validator for response_format-based structured output and a streaming rewind+retry path for OpenAI-compat streaming.

Motivation: users running in strict schema mode need deterministic validation errors while still benefiting from streaming; previously a schema failure in the middle of a stream simply produced a truncated or invalid payload and an opaque error.

This PR implements a low-overhead validator that runs on streamed chunks, detects schema divergence as early as possible, provides a compact machine-readable validation_failures payload, and when configured to 'rewind_on_schema_failure' will rewind the stream to the last safe token boundary, request an on-the-fly correction from the model (via a short re-prompt), and replay a corrected substream to the client.

Changes include: runtime validator, OpenAI-compat transport hooks, SDK helpers for Python/TS, docs + examples, and end-to-end tests.

Context & motivation: Multiple SDK consumers reported subtle mismatches between server-side session TTL propagation, streaming heartbeats, and SDK-side retry/keepalive semantics.

This caused short-lived production flakes where long-lived streaming clients were reauthorized unexpectedly or experienced silent stalls.

This PR harmonizes the contract across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs: 1) explicitly propagate server-issued session TTL to SDK session managers; 2) provide an optional lightweight heartbeat/ping helper on streaming handles to keep ephemeral sessions alive without user-managed timers; 3) expose a compact consumer-facing StreamFacade that simplifies reconnect + backoff + credential refresh for most application scenarios.

Seed synthetic traffic generator for demo dashboards (job + presets)

Problem: our demo tenant Console views (usage, latency percentiles, error analysis, cost breakdown) frequently show empty/flat graphs right before a live demo, and the distributions look obviously “fake” when we do a quick manual warm-up.

This PR introduces a synthetic traffic generator that continuously produces realistic, policy-driven demo traffic and emits the same telemetry path as real inference (usage + latency + error + trace hooks) so dashboards stay populated and believable.

What’s included: (1) a k8s CronJob + ad-hoc runner that hits the demo org’s routes via the public gateway (not direct ingestion) to exercise auth, rate limits, routing, and fallbacks; (2) preset configs (steady, executive-10min, spike, rollout-canary) to cover common demo narratives; (3) a small library for sampling realistic request shapes (prompt length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming mix, tool-calling frequency, structured output schema usage) and injecting controlled error rates (timeouts, 429s, tool validation failures) without overwhelming the tenant; (4) guardrails to ensure this can ONLY target the demo org/project allowlist and cannot run against prod/customer orgs.

Motivation: make the demo tenant resilient to “dashboard emptiness” and give SEs a one-command way to warm up the tenant prior to a call, while also generating data that makes cost/latency tradeoffs and reliability/fallback flows visible in the Console.

Rollout plan: merge behind DEMO_SYNTH_TRAFFIC_ENABLED, enable in demo env only, then let SRE tune the default schedule/caps after a week of observation.

Traffic is generated via the same public gateway path used by the demo app (so we get auth, quotas, routing, retries, and streaming behavior); requests are labeled with `x-redwood-traffic-source: demo_synth` and scenario tags (scenario=steady|spike|rollout_canary, feature=streaming|tool_calling|structured_output, region=us-east|eu-west).

Presets control: QPS target + jitter, streaming ratio, model mix weights, token length distributions, tool-call rate, structured output schema selection, and “controlled failure” knobs.

Guardrails: hard allowlist on org_id + project_id, environment check (must be DEMO env), and a max spend cap per hour (tokens + embeddings units) with immediate stop on breach.

Guardrails: hard allowlist on org_id + project_id, environment check (must be DEMO env), and a max spend cap per hour (tokens + embeddings units) with immediate stop on breach.

The CronJob uses a dedicated service account with egress restricted to the gateway; it does not have permissions to call internal admin endpoints.

Unit: distribution sampling (p50/p95 bounds), config parsing, allowlist enforcement; Integration (staging): `rw demo traffic run --preset executive-10min --dry-run=false` against staging demo org, verified dashboards populate within ~2–4 minutes; Load sanity: steady preset capped to avoid triggering 429s (unless explicitly enabled via spike preset).

Introduce RBAC anomaly detector, KMS usage ledger, and jurisdictional pin gate

Motivation: customers operating in regulated jurisdictions require stronger evidence about access decisions and KMS usage, plus automated detection of unusual privilege changes.

This PR adds three coordinated pieces: 1) an RBAC Anomaly Detector that samples policy decisions and surfaces statistical deviations (new service + control plane telemetry), 2) a KMS Usage Ledger that records per-tenant, per-key KMS call metadata for non-repudiable audit and residency verification, and 3) a Jurisdictional Pin Gate that enforces region-pin policies at the KMS allocation layer and emits canonical audit events for downstream compliance pipelines.

The goals are: reduce investigation time for policy breaches, provide provable KMS usage trails for compliance audits, and enforce region pin constraints at the decision point to avoid accidental cross-region key use.

introduce-reservoir-based-decentralized-scale-synthesizer

Motivation: production fleets see many short-lived microbursts from tenant traffic patterns which cause oscillatory autoscaling and wasted headroom.

This PR implements a lightweight reservoir-based "decentralized scale synthesizer" that runs alongside the existing autoscaler to smooth short spikes while preserving throughput guarantees and predictable tail latency.

Design summary: 1) each node maintains a small local reservoir credit accounting window that decays over time and is topped up by observed idle capacity; 2) the synthesizer aggregates ephemeral credits across replicas via a gossip-style delta protocol to create a soft, decentralized pool without a central control plane lock; 3) scaling decisions use a two-stage policy: local fast-path uses reservoir credits to accept short bursts without triggering scale-up, while the slow-path falls back to the cluster autoscaler when sustained demand exceeds reservoir thresholds.

Key properties: bounded amplification (reservoir caps per-tenant and per-node), graceful decay to avoid persistent overcommit, and deterministic backoff in preemption scenarios.

Telemetry and observability: added reservoir inflow/outflow metrics, reservoir_utilization_percentile by tenant, reservoir_credit_evictions, and a debug endpoint to snapshot local reservoir state.

Feature flags: env FLAG_RESERVOIR_SYNTHETIC=true enables the synthesizer and FLAG_RESERVOIR_GOSSIP controls gossip interval.

Backwards compatibility: autoscaler API unchanged, synthesizer registers as an optional operator.

Rollout plan: gated behind feature flags, start with canary on dedicated fleets for low-risk tenants, monitor latency and headroom burn rates for 72 hours, then progressive rollout.

Tests: unit tests for credit accounting and gossip reconciliation, integration tests simulating mixed-duration microbursts, and a synthetic benchmark showing 18% reduction in unnecessary scale-ups and 12% lower 99th percentile latency for bursty workloads in our lab.

Risk and mitigations: gossip divergence detected in tests fixed by introducing monotonic vector clocks and periodic full-state reconciliation.

Migration notes: no live migration required; operators can toggle off to immediately disable accepting reservoir credits.

See docs/design/reservoir-synthesizer.md for detailed algorithms and math.

Introduce hierarchical smoke-sampler and late-fail attenuator CI hook

Motivation: intermittent prompt-set failures (spikes driven by small cohorts) are causing noisy CI alerts and unnecessary rollbacks.

This PR adds a hierarchical smoke-sampler that builds a two-tier sampling plan (cohort-level followed by intra-cohort sampling) to increase coverage of high-variance prompt families while keeping smoke evaluation budgets bounded.

It also introduces a late-fail attenuator CI hook that downweights isolated failures that occur late in a sliding window and only escalates when failure weight persists across windows.

Design: sampler computes cohort disruption scores using historical eval variance and recent error-rate deltas; top-K cohorts are sampled proportionally to disruption with a minimum floor to avoid starvation.

The attenuator consumes per-prompt failure history and a tunable half-life to compute an effective failure weight; single-window blips are suppressed, sustained deviations trigger the existing quality gate.

Rollout plan: feature-flagged in CI config, dry-run for two weeks producing annotation-only reports, then opt-in for branch protection gating.

Tests: unit tests for sampler statistics, integration scenario with synthetic prompt drift, end-to-end CI scenario recorded in artifacts.

Checklist: implement sampler and hook, add feature flag, tests, docs and examples, update alerting thresholds.

Impact: should reduce noisy false positives and improve signal-to-noise for real regressions.

Backwards compatibility: disabled by default; no breaking changes.

Add shared KMS client abstraction with explicit timeouts + standardized retries

Summary: Introduces a shared KMS client abstraction used across control-plane + data-plane services to standardize timeouts, retries/backoff, and error mapping. The current KMS call sites implement timeouts inconsistently (or not at all) and several retry policies amplify load during provider-side latency spikes, which contributed to elevated 5xx during throttling events.

Key goals: - Make KMS dependency behavior predictable (bounded latency, bounded retries) - Provide a canonical error taxonomy for downstream policy (circuit breaker + degrade-mode followups) - Improve observability: metrics + structured log fields to enable on-call triage

Scope of this PR: - New library package `pkg/kmsclient` with:   - explicit deadlines for Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey/DescribeKey (per-operation defaults)   - retry policy w/ exponential backoff + jitter and a hard retry budget (max attempts and max elapsed)   - structured error mapping into a small set of categories (Timeout, Throttled, AccessDenied, NotFound, InvalidCiphertext, Internal, Unknown) - Minimal integration in two representative services to prove wiring + config surface (more migrations tracked in ENG-4823) - Adds unit tests for error mapping + retry budget behavior and a small fake KMS transport for deterministic tests

Non-goals: - Circuit breaker and degrade behavior (follow-up ENG-4824) - Metrics/tracing spans (follow-up PR; this keeps the wrapper API stable first) - Rotation / dual-read (ADR-008 work)

Configuration: - Defaults are conservative and aimed at production safety. Services can override via config, but values are validated and clamped to safe ranges in a later PR (ENG-4823 subtask). - Default budgets (v1):   - Encrypt/GenerateDataKey: timeout 2s, max attempts 3, max elapsed 3s   - Decrypt: timeout 2s, max attempts 2, max elapsed 2.5s (intentionally tighter to avoid fan-out storms) - Retryable errors: network timeouts, 5xx from provider SDK, explicit Throttling/RateExceeded

Error mapping: - Wrapper returns `KmsError` with fields: `category`, `provider_code`, `provider_message`, `is_retryable`, `request_id` (when available) - Logs should include: `kms.op`, `kms.category`, `kms.provider_code`, `kms.request_id`

Testing: - Unit tests for mapping (AWS-style error codes), retry budget accounting, and jitter range (non-deterministic aspects bounded via seeded RNG) - Adds a small integration-ish test using the fake transport to simulate throttle then success and assert we do not exceed max elapsed

Rollout plan: - Land wrapper, then migrate call sites incrementally behind a service-level config toggle where practical - SRE requested we ship metrics prior to broad rollout; follow-up PR will add `kms_client_latency_ms` histogram and `kms_client_errors_total` counter with tags

Refs: - Linear: ENG-4823 (wrapper), ENG-4822 (taxonomy) - Related support context: SUP-19377 (throttling leading to elevated 5xx) - ADR-007 draft in review (this PR implements the proposed API surface; final knobs may adjust slightly)

Screenshots / logs: - Example structured log emitted by wrapper on AccessDenied: `{"msg":"kms call failed","kms.op":"Decrypt","kms.category":"AccessDenied","kms.provider_code":"AccessDeniedException","kms.request_id":"2a4f...","err":"kms: access denied"}`

Checklist: - [x] Bounded timeouts for all KMS operations used in codebase today - [x] Standard retry policy with jitter - [x] Error taxonomy + mapping - [x] Unit tests + lint - [x] Docs in code (package README + godoc) - [ ] Metrics/tracing spans (next PR) - [ ] Circuit breaker integration (next PR)

dsid_01b76d9812a3477b8a37805830895a39__p.text:
Add dead-letter queue + guarded replay CLI for failed export batches

Summary: This PR introduces a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for audit export batches that fail delivery after exhausting retries, and adds an operator-facing replay tool with guardrails.

This is a reliability/safety feature for the SIEM-ready audit export beta (Splunk HEC / Datadog Logs / S3) to ensure we never silently drop events while still protecting the platform and customers from accidental replay storms.

Context / Motivation: During downstream outages (e.g., sustained 429s from Splunk HEC or 403s from mis-scoped Datadog keys), the exporter currently retries with backoff and then surfaces a per-destination error.

Without DLQ persistence we risk either (a) losing batches on process/queue churn or (b) having no safe operational path to replay specific failures once a customer fixes credentials/quotas.

ENG-5164 calls for a DLQ + replay tooling with explicit operator controls.

Design highlights: (1) DLQ record model: When a batch hits max_delivery_attempts OR we detect a non-retryable adapter error, we persist a DLQ record keyed by (tenant_id, export_config_id, checkpoint_range) and store the batch payload (newline-delimited JSON events) in object storage under a structured prefix.

DLQ record includes: dlq_id, created_at, tenant_id, export_config_id, destination_type, reason_code, reason_detail (redacted), first_event_ts, last_event_ts, event_count, byte_size, last_attempt_at, attempt_count, and a payload_ref. (2) At-least-once compatibility: Replays may cause duplicate deliveries.

We intentionally do not attempt exactly-once; downstream should dedup using event_id (per ADR on delivery semantics).

Replay CLI logs a reminder and requires an explicit --ack-duplicates flag. (3) Operator replay CLI: Adds bin/audit-exporter-replay (Go) to list DLQ items and replay in a controlled fashion.

Replay CLI logs a reminder and requires an explicit --ack-duplicates flag. (3) Operator replay CLI: Adds bin/audit-exporter-replay (Go) to list DLQ items and replay in a controlled fashion.

Guardrails include: required --tenant-id and --export-config-id; default is dry-run; interactive confirmation unless --yes is provided; bounded selection via --since/--until and --max-items; token-bucket rate limiting (--max-events-per-minute) to avoid spiking adapters; refuses to replay if export config is disabled OR if exporter feature flag is off for that tenant (unless --override-feature-flag is provided, which is restricted to on-call breakglass role). (4) Safety checks: Replay validates destination configuration hash matches the DLQ record by default (prevents replaying old payloads into a newly re-pointed sink).

Can be overridden with --ignore-config-hash-mismatch for incident response, but emits a prominent warning. (5) Redaction: DLQ reason_detail is run through the same redaction helper used by adapter logs to avoid accidentally persisting tokens/keys/PII.

Payloads contain audit events only (already subject to audit schema/PII policy); we do not include request/response bodies. (6) Observability: Adds metrics: audit_exporter_dlq_enqueued_total{tenant_id_hash,destination_type,reason_code}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_items{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_events{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_replay_total{result}, and audit_exporter_dlq_replay_latency_seconds.

Also adds structured logs for DLQ enqueue and replay runs (with correlation_id).

User-visible / Ops workflow: - When an adapter can’t deliver a batch and we exceed retry limits, exporter transitions the batch to DLQ and advances the live pipeline checkpoint to prevent system-wide backpressure. - On-call or Support can instruct customer to fix auth/limits, then run replay for the impacted tenant/config/time window. - Replay is incremental and rate-limited; any failures during replay are re-DLQ’d with a new reason_code (replay_failed_*).

Example commands: - List backlog: ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq list --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --until 2025-02-09T06:00:00Z - Dry-run replay (default): ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq replay --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --max-items 10 - Execute replay with explicit acknowledgements: ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq replay --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --max-items 50 --max-events-per-minute 12000 --ack-duplicates --yes Testing: - Unit tests for DLQ persistence, reason_code mapping, and redaction - Integration tests using adapter stubs: force 429/403/non-retryable to verify DLQ enqueue and payload roundtrip - Manual: replayed a synthetic backlog into Splunk stub with rate limiting and verified dedup by event_id Related: - Linear: ENG-5164 - ADR: delivery semantics and idempotency (at-least-once + event_id) - Support context: SUP-18531 (perceived missing events during throttling) Notes / Follow-ups: - Dashboard panels/alerts for DLQ backlog are tracked separately (we add metrics here, panels in observability-pack). - For beta, replay CLI is intended for on-call / SRE / Support escalation only; we are not exposing self-serve replay in Console.

If we advance, aren’t we skipping events?

Diego Santos (author): We’re not skipping generation; we’re persisting the batch payload + checkpoint range and treating replay as the at-least-once path.

Without advancing, a stuck tenant can backpressure worker resources and starve other tenants.

This matches ADR guidance: preserve payload, allow replay, accept duplicates.

Responses protocol adapter: stable fragment reassembly, toolcall boundaries, and seed handoff for OpenAI compatibility

Motivation: New OpenAI Responses variants expose streaming fragmentation semantics, RNG/seed hints, and richer metadata that must be faithfully represented in Redwood's Responses compatibility layer.

Without an adapter, hosted customers see reordering and truncated toolcall boundaries in streamed responses and cannot reproduce outputs when a seed is provided.

This PR implements a protocol adapter that stabilizes fragment reassembly, preserves explicit tool/function-call boundary markers in the stream, and forwards RNG/seed hints plus metadata passthrough to the sampling layer.

Design highlights: 1) Introduce lightweight fragment framing (frag_id, seq, final_flag) on the bridge to detect out-of-order chunks and perform deterministic reassembly with minimal buffering.

2) Emit and consume explicit toolcall boundary tokens at the adapter layer so function/tool callers receive well-formed call begin/end events even when the underlying runtime shards streams.

3) Map OpenAI-style "seed"/"deterministic" hint fields to an internal RNG-hint header and expose a seed proxy that pins sampling when requested for reproducible debug runs.

4) Preserve response-level metadata (request_id, model_attrs, user_metadata) by passthrough on the adapter and tag primary streaming frames with metadata headers so the console and observability pipelines retain attribution.

5) Fail-open fallback: when fragment integrity cannot be verified within a configurable timeout, the adapter falls back to per-chunk best-effort delivery and flags the event in logs/metrics.

Implementation notes: Changes are concentrated in services/bridge/openai_adapter.go (adapter logic and framing), runtime/stream/framer.go (framing helpers), runtime/stream/reassembly.go (reassembly state machine), runtime/sampling/seed_proxy.go (seed handoff and validation), api/compat/responses_adapter_test.go (unit/integration tests), and docs/compat/openai-responses.md (compatibility guide).

The adapter is feature-flagged under "openai_responses_adapter_v2" and gated behind a canary rollout.

Tests and validation: added deterministic integration tests that replay recorded fragment orders, end-to-end tests against an OpenAI-compat harness, and a small perf canary to verify latency impact under 99th-percentile SLOs.

Observability: new metrics added: adapter.frag_reassembly.latency_ms, adapter.frag_reassembly.reorders, adapter.toolcall.boundary_mismatches, and adapter.seed_forward.count.

dsid_01ca27f5a5b142d7b897f8f275c14044__p.text:
introduce slab-grafting reclaimer and spill-rate cap to reduce KV cache fragmentation and spill storms

Motivation: In high-concurrency tenant workloads we continue to see transient spill storms driven by large numbers of small, fragmented slot allocations.

These storms increase peak GPU memory usage and cause cascading evictions that harm latency.

This PR introduces two orthogonal mitigations: (1) a slab-grafting reclaimer that coalesces adjacent free slots into larger usable extents with low CPU overhead, and (2) a spill-rate cap controller that rate-limits and smooths background spill operations to avoid sudden IO spikes.

Design: slab-grafting is implemented as a background, incremental pass that scans per-shard free lists and attempts opportunistic graft operations when fragmentation score exceeds a threshold.

Grafting is lock-free with respect to normal alloc/free paths by using a CAS-based two-phase promotion that marks ranges as 'staging' before atomically linking them into larger slabs.

The spill-rate cap is a token-bucket controller in the KV spill scheduler; it enforces a soft cap on MB/sec of spill throughput and exposes a spill_smoothing_window_ms knob.

When cap is hit, the scheduler prefers reclaiming contiguous grafted slabs and defers noncritical spill tasks.

Compatibility: the grafting path is gated behind a runtime flag enable_slab_grafting and defaults off for older clusters; the spill cap has a conservative default of 128 MB/s but is tunable per-deployment and can be disabled.

Testing: unit tests validate graft correctness across races and simulated concurrent frees; a stress harness (tools/kv_stress) demonstrates a 45% reduction in maximum concurrent spill IO during mixed-read/write tenant workloads, and a 12% P99 latency improvement on the generation path in our benchmark-lab scenarios.

Rollout plan: staged canary to 10% of pods for 48h, monitor memory residency and spill_io_mbps metrics, then 50% for 24h, then global.

Related work: follows the fragmentation detection work in ENG-3983 and complements the asynchronous compactor (ENG-4620).

Known limitations: grafting is not effective for highly interleaved small live objects; in those cases we still rely on the compactor and eviction heuristics.

Safety: feature flags and conservative defaults provided; metrics to watch: kv.fragmentation_score, kv.graft_ops, kv.spill_mbps, kv.eviction_count.

Safety: feature flags and conservative defaults provided; metrics to watch: kv.fragmentation_score, kv.graft_ops, kv.spill_mbps, kv.eviction_count.

dsid_01d02d95db18420a97b2f63aa502656e__p.text:
runtime: make optimization config applier idempotent + retry-safe (partial rollout safeguards)

Context: As part of Safe apply + rollback for Optimization Configs, the control plane will issue apply operations that may be retried (network timeouts, controller restarts) and can be delivered out-of-order relative to worker restarts and shard movement. Prior implementation applied configs as a best-effort "set current" and would re-run side effects on every delivery (cache invalidation, batcher reinit), which increased tail latency and could leave mixed worker states during partial rollout. This PR makes the runtime Optimization Config applier idempotent and resilient to retries, and adds explicit safeguards for partial rollout states.

What changed: 1) Introduced apply_operation_id and deterministic apply keying. The runtime now consumes ApplyOptimizationConfig(scope, version, apply_operation_id, reason) and records a durable ApplyRecord per (scope, version). If the same apply_operation_id is delivered again, the operation is treated as a no-op after verifying the recorded checksum. 2) Added a small durable state store (RuntimeOptimizationConfigState) to persist last_desired_version, last_applied_version, last_apply_operation_id, and an apply_status enum (PENDING/APPLIED/FAILED). This survives worker restarts and prevents "double apply" side effects after process crashes. 3) Side-effect gating: cache invalidation and batch scheduler resets now run only on transition from one applied version to another, and are skipped on idempotent retries. 4) Partial rollout safeguards: if a worker receives an apply for an older version than its recorded desired_version, it will reject it with a conflict response unless reason=ROLLBACK (explicit rollback) or allow_downgrade=true from control plane. This prevents late/stale apply messages from reintroducing a regressed version mid-rollout. 5) Repair behavior: if apply_status is FAILED for the same (scope, version) and the controller retries with a new apply_operation_id, the runtime will re-attempt apply (previously a failed apply could wedge workers until manual restart). 6) Observability: added metrics and structured logs to make retry/no-op/conflict behavior visible: optimization_config_apply_total{result=applied|noop|conflict|failed}, optimization_config_apply_duration_ms, and optimization_config_state_gauge{state}. All are tagged with tenant/model/region/config_version/apply_operation_id (apply_operation_id only in logs to avoid high cardinality metrics).

Why this is safe: The new behavior is strictly more conservative. Duplicate deliveries become no-ops, stale messages are rejected, and only explicit rollbacks can downgrade. Persisted state ensures crashes don’t cause reapplication storms (and the associated cache flush latency spikes). Unit + integration tests cover retry ordering, crash/restart, and conflict semantics.

Follow-ups: - Control plane rollout controller will start supplying apply_operation_id everywhere (tracked in ENG-4824). - Console will surface conflict/failed reasons using the error codes introduced here. - We should consider promoting apply_operation_id into trace spans once tracing propagation is in place for the apply pipeline.

Noah Patel (author): Yes, this is local to the runtime pod (same path as other small runtime state; falls back to in-memory if not writable). If the pod is rescheduled, we lose the record, but idempotency still holds per-process; the controller retries will reapply cleanly. The durable store mainly prevents re-running side effects after a crash/restart on the same node and avoids repeated cache flushes. apply_operation_id is logs-only; metrics are tagged with tenant/model/region/config_version and result.

If the controller pauses/resumes the same operation, desired_version doesn’t change, so no conflict. paged-kv: implement soft-pin block allocator and reuse heuristics to reduce fragmentation

Motivation: long-lived KV cache entries and block fragmentation were causing elevated tail latency and increased GPU memory pressure under mixed-sequence workloads.

This PR introduces a 'soft pin' block allocation strategy and stronger reuse heuristics for the paged KV block manager to reduce allocation churn and eviction storms.

Summary of changes: 1) New soft-pin concept for blocks: blocks can be marked soft-pinned when referenced by in-flight decode contexts; they are excluded from immediate eviction but eligible for reuse by same-owner contexts to avoid duplication.

2) Segregated free lists per size class with compact LRU buckets to improve reuse locality.

3) Eviction ranking that factors in last-access timestamp, owner affinity, and live-kv-count to avoid evicting hot multi-token KV pages.

4) GC/compaction path to coalesce small free fragments when fragmentation exceeds threshold.

5) Runtime knobs: kv.soft_pin_v2 (bool), kv.free_list_threshold (int), kv.compact_fraction (float).

Design notes: the soft-pin is a lightweight per-block ref-bit plus ownership tag; ownership is used only as a hint for reuse and does not bypass safety checks.

Reuse is conservative: blocks reclaimed for reuse must not have active external pointers.

Benchmarks: local microbench (mixed chat + completion load, seq distribution 8-1024) shows 10-14% reduction in p99 token-latency and ~12% throughput improvement on T4-equivalent nodes; memory overhead reduced ~6% due to less duplicated KV pages.

Rollout plan: feature gated, canary on 5% of hosted traffic, ramp to 50% after 48h if perf signals stable.

Backout: revert kv.soft_pin_v2 or set kv.free_list_threshold high.

Related work: follow-ups planned to integrate with continuous batching's slot-aware scheduling to further co-locate reuses.

Linear tickets: ENG-2143, ENG-2178.

Risks: potential subtle race during concurrent eviction and decoder handoff; mitigated with additional CAS checks and stress tests.
