Introduce TimeWarp RAG Simulator quickstart: synthetic user & structured-output linter

Motivation: Reproducing user-facing RAG regressions that depend on network latency, index freshness, or multi-tool interactions is time-consuming.

This quickstart introduces the TimeWarp simulator — a lightweight local harness that lets engineers run deterministic, time-scaled RAG scenarios and assert structured outputs against expected contracts.

The goal is a low-friction developer loop to reproduce flaky tool-calls, evaluate output stability under synthetic delays, and run quick regressions in CI.

What this PR adds: 1) quickstarts/timewarp-simulator/README.md — end-to-end guide and expected workflows; 2) a compact TypeScript runner (runner/ts/) that drives synthetic user sessions with configurable latency/timewarp factors and replayable corpora; 3) a structured-output linter (examples/linting/structured-output-linter.py) that validates JSON/YAML responses against field-level contracts and fuzzy string expectations; 4) telemetry probes (telemetry/probes.yaml) and a CI smoke job (ci/smoke-timewarp.yml) that runs a short scenario on PRs to catch regressions; 5) docs site registration (docs/quickstarts.yml and docs/snippets/timewarp-setup.md) so quickstart appears in the docs sidebar.

Security & privacy: The runner uses seedable, local-only corpora (examples/playback/sample-corpus.json) and never ships customer data; a note in the README explains sanitization for real-indexed corpora.

Quickstart highlights and commands: - Install node and python (README includes minimal versions). - From the quickstart dir: npm ci && npm run build && node dist/run.js --corpus examples/playback/sample-corpus.json --timewarp 0.5 --seed 42 This runs a session that simulates accelerated token/latency pacing (0.5x wall clock). - To run with a 2x slow-down: --timewarp 2.0 - Lint responses: python3 examples/linting/structured-output-linter.py --input out/session-001.json --schema quickstarts/timewarp-simulator/contracts/session-schema.yaml - CI smoke: ci/smoke-timewarp.yml runs the runner against a short scenario and fails the job if structured-output linter finds contract divergences.

Developer notes & checklist: - ✅ Deterministic seeds added to runner and sample corpus for reproducibility. - ✅ Minimal telemetry hooks (span ids + latency histograms) added so SRE can wire into existing dashboards. - ✅ Docs snippets and usage examples included with copyable CLI commands. - ✅ Small sample corpus and a guide for sanitizing real corpora are included. - Known limitations: The simulator is not a substitute for full-scale load testing; it targets functional/regression scenarios and structured-output stability.

It currently supports HTTP-based tool stubs and the Redwood hosted API compatibility layer; adding grpc tool stubs is tracked in ENG-3330.

Migration/upgrade notes: The quickstart is opt-in; it does not change runtime behavior.

To adopt, teams can copy the quickstart folder into their repos or reference the runner as a submodule.

Add reservoired burst-accountant and steady-window SLO profiles for Dedicated fleets

Customers observed intermittent microburst patterns that repeatedly pushed Dedicated tenants past short-term P95 latency SLAs despite healthy long-window utilization. This PR introduces a reservoired burst-accountant and a configurable steady-window SLO profile to explicitly decouple short burst allowances from steady throughput guarantees.

What this changes: added a credit reservoir model (per-tenant, per-fleet) that accrues credit when observed usage is below a configurable steady-window baseline, and draws down when short-term bursts exceed nominal throughput. Credits are persisted in the reservation ledger with TTL and soft-eviction semantics. A new steady-window SLO profile (window length, baseline qps, burn-rate caps, recovery rate) can be attached to tenant reservations and accepted by the autoscaler and admission controller. The admission controller now consults the accountant to allow transient overcommit within the credit budget, and emits telemetry so ops can see effective burst headroom and expected exhaustion times.

Why: previous autoscaling heuristics conflated short-term spike handling with long-window capacity planning, leading to noisy scale-ups and SLA flapping. The reservoir model reduces unnecessary scale churn, improves tail latency consistency, and provides an audit trail for transient overages.

Compatibility and opt-in: new behavior is gated behind the feature flag "reservoired_burst_accountant" and is enabled by default for Dedicated fleets started after the release date. Existing fleets will remain on traditional burst heuristics unless opt-in is performed via the Console or API. Backward-compatible admission paths exist: if the accountant data is unavailable, the system falls back to current conservative limits.

Testing and validation: unit tests for ledger persistence, integration tests simulating realistic burst profiles, and a small-scale canary (10 fleets) run in perf-lab. Load tests show P95 latency improvements of 12-18% on bursty workloads and reduced autoscale events by ~28%.

Rollback plan: revert feature flag (ops) to disable accountant and fall back to baseline burst limits. Post-merge tasks: telemetry dashboard, Console opt-in UI, and a follow-up PR to add a per-tenant dry-run mode that reports but does not enforce credit draws.

Introduce inference health scorer and token-cost forecast panel

Motivation: Production teams want a single, explainable signal that summarizes invocation health (latency, cost, cache-warmth, model-fallbacks) and a short-term forecast of token burn to reduce noisy alerts during predictable bursts. This PR introduces a lightweight per-invocation 'inference_health_score' (0-100) plus a token-cost forecast panel that surfaces 1h/6h/24h EWMA forecasts and a confidence band.

What this changes (high level):
- Instrumentation: runtime emits 'inference_health_score', and additional tags: token_cohort, kernel_slot, hw_tier, prefix_warmth. Implemented in serving/telemetry/health_scorer.rs and runtime/tracing/span_enricher.cpp.
- Aggregation/worker: observability/pipelines/forecast_worker.go computes per-tenant EWMA forecasts for token-cost (tokens/sec and token-cost/sec) and writes forecast series to the metrics cache. Forecasts use an EWMA with adaptive alpha (short/long windows) and a confidence band from recent variance.
- Dashboard: grafana/dashboards/inference_health_and_forecast.json adds: health-summary heatmap, forecast sparkline (1h/6h/24h), cohorted bar (by token_cohort), and a causal-log-mosaic link column that deep-links into the trace inspector.
- Alerts: alerting/rules/forecast_slo_rules.yaml includes a forecast-aware alert rule that defers paging if projected 1h burn is within hysteresis threshold; it still fires if the health_score drops below 30 or if a critical fallback rate is observed.

Design notes:
- health_score composition: 40% latency SLO distance, 25% token-cost z-score, 20% prefix_warmth (higher is better), 10% kernel_queue_penalty, 5% recent-model-fallback-rate. The metric is normalized to 0-100 with guarded NaN handling. The algorithm is intentionally transparent (implemented as a deterministic rule in health_scorer.rs) to make RCA easier.
- Forecasting: we opted for EWMA-based forecasting to keep compute cheap in the ingest tier. The worker maintains short (1h), medium (6h), and long (24h) windows and exposes a 'forecast_confidence' derived from window variance.
- Alert tuning: new rule adds a 'forecast_quiet_window' if the projected burn explains the deviation; an 'explainability' label is attached listing the dominant contributor (e.g., "arrival_profile", "kv_cache_cold").

Backward compatibility & opt-out: default is enabled. For Dedicated/Private customers we provide an opt-out via config: observability.features.health_scorer=false. Metric names are stable and documented in docs/observability/metric_catalog.md.

Testing & validation:
- Unit tests: health_scorer unit tests cover composition edge cases, NaN handling, and bucket assignment (tests/health_scorer_test.rs).
- Integration: forecast_worker was run in a staging replay (replaybench) for a 72h synthetic workload; dashboard panels validated against the replay and matched expected forecasts within 3% on average.
- Load: worker CPU and memorystore usage measured on staging 2x baseline with no observable impact on ingest pipeline; added a 50ms budget cap per-window evaluation to avoid tail amplification.

perf: cross-batch dequant fusion with amortized per-token rescale for mixed-precision kernels

Motivation: Long-context workloads show fragmentation across microbatches that prevent effective dequant fusion and cause repeated dequant/rescale operations per token.

This PR introduces a cross-batch dequant fusion pass plus an amortized per-token rescale step that cooperates with the KV cache and continuous batching coordinator to reduce redundant dequant work for INT8/FP8 mixed-precision serving.\n\nSummary of changes: implemented a new CrossBatchDequanter that tracks compatible contiguous microbatch windows and emits a fused dequant operation for stacked tokens; added an AmortizedRescale operator that defers fine-grained scale adjustments until token groups exceed a stability threshold; extended the scheduler with a cross-batch affinity hint and modified the KV cache interface to expose per-layer scale metadata needed by the fused path.

Also added kernel-level fastpaths for fused int8->fp16 conversion targeting long prefix reuse patterns.\n\nDesign notes: the fused path is opt-in behind a runtime feature flag (RUNTIME_FUSED_DEQUANT).

When enabled the scheduler annotates queued requests with batch-affinity tags; CrossBatchDequanter periodically probes the queue to form mergeable windows constrained by latency SLO heuristics.

AmortizedRescale computes a combined scale factor and only applies per-token micro-adjustments when the cumulative quantization error crosses a configurable threshold (defaults tuned from benchmarks).

Compatibility: falls back to existing per-request dequant for heterogeneous model variants and when KV cache indicates incompatible scale signatures.\n\nBenchmarks: microbench on p4d.24xlarge with a 16k context evaluation harness showed up to 22% throughput improvement and 18% average token-latency reduction on customer-like chat load (95th percentile latency remained within SLO).

FP8/INT8 combined workloads saw better utilization due to fewer kernel launches and improved KV cache hit patterns.

Detailed numbers included in /docs/perf/crossbatch-dequant-run-2026-02-20.md.\n\nTesting: unit tests for CrossBatchDequanter and AmortizedRescale (kernel emulation mode), end-to-end CI smoke against the runtime with synthetic traffic, and a canary rollout configuration for Dedicated.

Stress tests included kv-cache warm/cold cycles and continuous-batching scenarios.

Differential audit sampling + KMS call-path reconciliation for RBAC v2 operator scope

Motivation: Reduce sensitive-audit volume while preserving forensic fidelity and ensuring per-call KMS provenance for operator-scoped actions.

This PR implements a differential audit-sampling layer (route + risk aware) integrated with an end-to-end KMS call-path reconciler to ensure any sampled event carries provable KMS metadata that can be traced back to the operator credential used.

Changes include a sampling policy engine, hooks in the RBACv2 enforcer to emit sampling signals, and a background reconciler that annotates audit events with KMS proofs and retries failed attestations.

Rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag rbacv2.diff_audit_sampling; default off for enterprise accounts.

Add RAG mosaic authoring stubs and live-preview quickstart

Introduce a compact quickstart that demonstrates a 'mosaic' authoring pattern for RAG scenarios: template stubs, a live preview server, telemetry probes, and a devcontainer for local onboarding.
Motivation and summary: Add a lightweight quickstart that shows authors how to compose retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) scenarios using a 'mosaic' layout: small, composable step templates (retrieval, transform, tool-call, finalization) that can be arranged and previewed in real time. This is targeted at developer-first product teams who want fast iteration cycles when authoring multi-step agents and tool-calling flows. The quickstart includes: 1) starter templates for step types, 2) a tiny live-preview server that streams intermediate step outputs into a mosaic UI, 3) telemetry probes and example probes for Redwood Console, 4) a devcontainer and scripts to run locally, and 5) CI e2e smoke tests.

What changed (high-level): commits: - Add mosaic authoring templates and README (initial scaffolding) - Add live-preview server (FastAPI + SSE) and browser UI - Wire telemetry probe hooks and example telemetry config - Add devcontainer, Makefile and local-run scripts - Add CI smoke test that runs quickstart e2e in headless mode - Docs site section and short how-to guide

Changed areas/files (representative): - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/README.md (new authoring guide and examples) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/templates/*.yaml (retrieval/transform/tool/output stubs) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/live-preview/server.py (SSE endpoints + example runner) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/live-preview/static/index.html (mosaic UI) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/devcontainer.json + .devcontainer/Dockerfile - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/telemetry/probes.yaml - .github/workflows/quickstart-e2e.yml (added smoke job) - docs/site/content/quickstarts/rag-mosaic.md (documentation and screenshots)

Usage and run instructions (short): 1) git checkout feature/rag-mosaic-authoring-live-preview 2) cd quickstarts/rag-mosaic 3) ./dev.sh start (boots local index, preview server, and sample index) 4) Open http://localhost:8080 to interact with mosaic editor and live preview The quickstart ships with a small seeded index (sqlite + json files) and an in-memory mock tool for safe local iteration.

Design notes and rationale: - Mosaic layout: each step emits a compact envelope {type, summary, tokens_used, result_preview}. The UI displays envelopes tiled so authors can quickly inspect how retrieval, rerank, transform, and tool calls interact. - Live preview uses SSE to avoid full-page polling; server-side runner replays a seeded conversation and emits step-level deltas to the UI. This mirrors production tracing while remaining lightweight for local runs. - Telemetry probes: small hooks are emitted from the runner with route and token-level metadata; default probes are no-op but wired to Redwood Console examples in telemetry/probes.yaml. - Templates: YAML-based step templates were chosen for readability and copy/paste ergonomics in docs and repos. Templates include sensible defaults for caching/batching hints and an example quantization/throughput note.

Testing and CI: - Added a headless CI job quickstart-e2e that launches the preview server, runs a scripted interaction via curl/WebSocket, and validates expected envelopes are emitted. - Initial runs flagged a flaky timing issue in the SSE client; fixed by adding a small backoff and a readiness probe in server.py. The quickstart is additive and isolated under quickstarts/rag-mosaic. - Risk: SSE behavior might differ across browsers; added guidance in README with fallback polling option and a small compatibility test in the e2e job.

Signed Terraform Plan Artifacts and Helm-diff Rollback Gating

Context and motivation:
This PR implements a reproducible, signed artifact workflow for Terraform plans and a Helm-chart-diff-driven rollback gating mechanism for the private installer CI/CD. Recent customer upgrades highlighted two operational gaps: (1) lack of a verifiable plan artifact to attest exactly what will change during an upgrade, and (2) upgrades failing to generate deterministic rollback anchors when chart/value drift occurs in airgapped environments.

Summary of changes:
- Generate a canonical, reproducible terraform plan JSON during staging, canonicalize it (strip timestamps, sort maps), and sign the blob with cosign using the org KMS key. Signed artifacts are uploaded to the release bucket under /plans/<release>/<cluster>.plan.json.sig and recorded in the release manifest.
- Add a lightweight plan-verifier binary (tools/plan-verifier) used in CI and in the installer preflight to validate signatures and ensure the on-cluster state matches the plan fingerprint before applying.
- Add a Helm chart diff preflight that computes a normalized diff between current deployed chart+values and the candidate release, identifies changed template keys that are rollback-risky (stateful migration hooks, volume changes), and produces a rollback anchor entry to include in the release manifest.
- CI: new pipeline step ci/pipelines/verify-signed-plan.yml to gate merges for private-installer changes that touch upgrade paths. The pipeline verifies signatures, runs the helm-diff preflight against a live staging cluster simulator, and publishes the artifacts.
- Docs: docs/upgrade-runbook.md extended with a signed-plan troubleshooting section and instructions for on-prem operators on how to rotate signing keys.

Design notes and security posture:
- Artifact signing uses cosign with KMS-backed keys (AWS KMS / GCP KMS interchangeable). The plan JSON canonicalization is intentionally strict: deterministic ordering of resources and consistent provider addresses to ensure reproducible fingerprinting across CI runs.
- The plan artifact and helm-diff anchor are stored with provenance metadata (git ref, pipeline id, signer id) and included in the release manifest so the installer can make allowlist decisions during an airgapped apply.
- The preflight runs in two modes: CI-mode (simulator) and runtime-mode (installer preflight). The latter defaults to fail-closed when signatures or anchors are absent, but an operator flag --allow-unsigned-upgrades is available for troubleshooting with audit logging.

How to test locally:
1) ./scripts/generate-plan.sh --cluster test-cluster --out /tmp/plan.json (creates canonical plan JSON)
2) ./scripts/sign-plan.sh /tmp/plan.json (produces /tmp/plan.json.sig)
3) tools/plan-verifier verify --plan /tmp/plan.json --sig /tmp/plan.json.sig --kms-key $KMS_KEY
4) Run helm diff preflight: tools/helm-diff-preflight --current ./staging/chart --candidate ./charts/private-installer --values ./staging/values.yaml
5) Execute the CI simulation job locally: ./ci/local-run verify-signed-plan.yml

Migration and rollout plan:
- Feature is behind a flag (ENABLE_SIGNED_PLANS). We will enable CI gating for all release branches for two weeks in staged mode. During the first week, the pipeline will publish signed artifacts but not block merges; during week two it will block merges if signatures are missing.
- Operators will be notified via release notes and the private-installer Slack channel with instructions for key rotation and preflight diagnostics.

Related work and references:
- Related Linear tickets: ENG-7382 (plan attestation), ENG-7390 (helm rollback anchors).
- Inspired by upstream reproducible-plan work and cosign best practices.

- [x] CI pipeline integration and tests
- [x] Docs + runbook updates

Sliding canary with composite SLO gates, shadow validation and automated rollback choreography

Motivation: Customers running mixed-quality-sensitive workloads asked for a rollout mode that can: (1) evaluate live traffic quality (semantic/regression metrics) alongside traditional SLOs (p50/p95 latency, error rate), (2) apply a gradual sliding window increase in traffic rather than fixed steps, and (3) wire automated rollback choreography when any composite gate trips while preserving an audit trail and optional shadow replay for offline bisect.

This PR implements a new rollout strategy named 'sliding-canary' in the rollout controller and adds telemetry-driven composite gates that aggregate signals across latency, error rate, and configured application-level quality checks (e.g., eval-set regression score). The strategy supports: sliding traffic ramps (percent per minute), safety holdpoints with manual approval, shadow capture for failing slices, and coordinated rollback with tokenized rollback-playbook events for operator playbooks.

Key user-visible changes:
- New rollout.strategy.type = "sliding-canary" with fields: start_percent, max_percent, slide_rate_per_min, hold_points[], composite_gates[]. Each composite_gate can reference latency/error thresholds and quality metric expressions.
- New API endpoints: POST /rollouts/:id/snapshot and POST /rollouts/:id/force-hold for operator intervention.
- Shadow capture toggle at rollout level to mirror traffic for offline replay and automated bisect.
- Automated rollback choreography: when a composite gate trips, controller emits a rollback token and sends a structured event to the playbook queue; optional dry-run replays can be configured.

Design summary:
- Controller: implements time-windowed sliding window sampler (defaults to 60s windows) collecting per-route aggregated signals. Composite gates evaluate historical windows with configurable decay to prevent single-spike noise.
- Telemetry: added new rollup metrics (rollout.window_latency_p95, rollout.window_error_rate, rollout.window_quality_regression) and tags for rollout_id, cohort. These feed into the composite gate evaluator and the console dashboards.
- Shadowing: lightweight capture stores request metadata + model-output fingerprint in compressed sstable and emits a pointer to object storage. Replay harness reuses existing replay infra but tags traces with original rollout cohort for bisect.
- Safety: built-in backoff policy on rollback that respects operator holdpoints and supports an autorecover mode if upstream transient issue resolves (configurable cooldown).

Migration/backcompat: existing rollout configs are unchanged; sliding-canary is opt-in. Controllers running older versions ignore sliding-canary rollouts and return a validation error prompting users to upgrade. Migration doc included.

Tests & CI: unit tests for gate evaluation, e2e integration tests for sliding ramp behavior and rollback choreography, and a small load test simulating mixed-quality degradation.

introduce-econ-orchard-mini-sampler-and-quant-curator

Motivation: This PR adds the 'Econ Orchard' suite — a compact, production-safe set of tools that generate conservative default batching/caching presets, a lightweight micro-sampler for workload-shaped telemetry, and a small quantization profile curator to recommend safe quant variants per SKU. The goal is to accelerate onboarding for customers who want unit-economics-aware defaults without running large-scale profiling jobs.

What this PR does (single continuous description): Implements a mini-sampler agent (orchard-sampler) that runs lightweight request sampling in the runtime path to collect sequence-length distributions, prefix reuse ratios, and short-term tail latency histograms; introduces a Quant Curator service that maps observed telemetry to a small set of tested quantization presets with a safety score; adds an econ-defaults generator that synthesizes tiered batch/cache/quant defaults per deployment SKU (burst, steady, latency-sensitive) and exposes them via the CLI and the Console defaults API; includes a new 'unit-econ quick-checker' CLI command that simulates expected cost/latency delta for candidate presets against recorded traces.

Files and surface changes: - runtime/orchard/mini_sampler.py: sampling agent with extremely small overhead path and failsafe circuit. - runtime/orchard/kv_prefetch_policy.py: new conservative prefetch policy for small caches. - optimizer/quant_curator/*.py: mapping and scoring logic for quant presets. - cli/econ_tool.py: `redwood econ quick-check` and `redwood econ apply-defaults` commands. - docs/quickstarts/econ-orchard.md: one-page guide and safety guidance. - tests/unit/test_mini_sampler.py, tests/integration/test_econ_cli.sh: end-to-end smoke tests.

Operational safeguards: sampling runs at 0.5% by default (configurable), includes an opt-out header for privacy-sensitive customers, and uses moving-window aggregation with caps to avoid memory blowups. The Quant Curator only recommends profiles that were previously exercised on a compatible architecture; every recommendation carries a 'safety_score' and default action is conservative (prefer higher precision when score < 0.9).

Add residency-proofing middleware and audit entropy hashing

Motivation: Customers operating under strong data residency constraints need cryptographic proof that KMS operations and key usage occurred in the expected region without exposing deterministic audit identifiers that could be used to correlate requests across tenants. This PR introduces a residency-proofing middleware that records signed, region-anchored statements for KMS operations and an audit entropy-hashing layer that salts audit identifiers before logging to reduce cross-tenant correlation risk.

What this change does: Adds a lightweight middleware component in the frontdoor service that: (1) validates KMS provider region against tenant policy, (2) emits a residency proof blob signed by the platform's attestation key, and (3) attaches a short immutable nonce reference to the outgoing audit envelope. Introduces an audit hashing pipeline stage that applies HMAC-SHA256 with a per-tenant entropy seed (rotated periodically) to resource identifiers before they hit the audit log. Adds RBAC v2 enforcement rules that require the new residency-proof scope for operators who can override region pins. Feature-flagged rollout: residency-proofing is behind feature flag feature.residency_proofs and audit-hash behind feature.audit_entropy_hashing.

Risk and mitigation: New cryptographic material is added (attestation key and per-tenant entropy seeds). Keys are provisioned via the KMS provisioning flow and stored in the secrets store with restricted ACLs. CI includes integration tests that exercise seed rotation and residency proof verification. We ship a migration that backfills proof metadata where possible but does not change existing audit formats unless the feature flag is enabled.

Introduce Econ Optimizer Runbook with Auto-apply Curation

Motivation: Customers repeatedly ask for safe, repeatable ways to adopt cost-reduction defaults (batching, prefix caching) and curated quantization profiles while preserving serving SLOs.

This PR introduces a human-readable runbook + an 'auto-apply' curation flow for tenant defaults that is conservative by default and observable via telemetry.

The runbook ties together: 1) declarative preset profiles (batch/cache/quant) for common workload archetypes; 2) a dry-run simulator that evaluates unit-economics and SLO risk; 3) an opt-in auto-apply path that materializes safe changes as tenant overrides; 4) telemetry hooks and audit records for traceability.

Design summary:
- Presets: new YAML schema under services/econ-runbook/presets/ describing batch_shape, cache_policy, target_quant_profile, acceptable_latency_delta_pct, and rollout_guard.

Presets map to tags (e.g., "interactive-small", "batching-high-thr").
- Dry-run simulator: leverages existing workload traces to simulate token-cost, GPU utilization, and 95/99 latency shifts; generates an econ delta report with suggested confidence bands.
- Auto-apply: an operator-approved flow.

A runbook action produces a proposed tenant override set stored in the config service; the operator may 'apply' which triggers a canary rollout (5% traffic) followed by a 1h observation window.

Automatic rollback if latency/SLO breach or error rate spike > 2x baseline.
- Telemetry: new metrics and spans (econ.runbook.proposal.*, econ.runbook.apply.*, econ.runbook.simulation.summary) with links to correlated traces and the tenant audit log entry.
- Quant profiles: introduce a curated whitelist of quant strategies (q8_qat, q4_vnni-lite, q6_mixed) tied to model families and validated by the simulator.

For model families not whitelisted, the runbook recommends fallback-safe profiles.
- Safety: rollout_guard enforces 'no more than X% unit cost reduction per 24h' and refuses aggressive quant profiles for low-latency SLO tenants.

Add Terraform plan guard and Helm airgap shim with migration simulator

Motivation: Private/on-prem customers running air-gapped or tightly controlled environments need deterministic upgrade outcomes.

Two common failure modes we've seen in incidents are (1) unintended Terraform resource churn during apply and (2) missing chart artifacts or image references in airgapped clusters.

This PR introduces three coordinated pieces: a Terraform plan guard (installer/terraform/modules/plan_guard) that enforces an allowlist and diff threshold before apply; a Helm airgap shim (installer/helm/airgap-shim) that stages and validates all chart assets and image digests ahead of rolling upgrades; and a migration simulator tool (installer/tools/migration_simulator) that can run DB/KV schema migrations in dry-run mode against a snapshot to detect incompatible changes before an in-place upgrade.

Summary of changes: - installer/terraform/modules/plan_guard: new module that wraps terraform plan/apply with a preflight validator (configurable thresholds, allow/deny rules, and auto-approve gating). - installer/helm/airgap-shim: small utility and chart hooks to bundle required tarballs and image digests, validate registry replacement maps, and produce a signed asset manifest for offline clusters. - installer/tools/migration_simulator: Go binary that can replay migration SQL/transform logic against a detached DB snapshot and emit a regression report with row-level checks and schema diffs. - installer/docs/upgrade-playbook.md: updated step-by-step including how to run the plan guard, use the airgap shim, run the migration simulator, and perform the orchestrated rollback if needed. - ci: added tests for plan_guard logic and a unit test harness for migration simulator using SQLite snapshots.

Backwards compatibility: Plan guard is opt-in via a top-level flag in the Terraform root (guard_enabled = false by default) so existing automation is unaffected.

The Helm shim is additive; it exposes an alternate release flow for airgapped installs.

Migration simulator does not change runtime migration code; it is strictly a preflight tool.

The Helm shim is additive; it exposes an alternate release flow for airgapped installs.

Testing and verification: - Local integration tested against a reproducible example cluster and a synthetic DB snapshot (see installer/examples/airgap-smoke). - Terraform plan guard tested with scenarios: benign diff, resource rename, and unexpected deletion; guard thresholds behaved as expected, blocking destroy-heavy plans. - Helm shim validated on an offline KIND cluster (chart assets served from local registry) and through OCI tarball manifests. - CI: unit tests and a small integration job passed on re-run; one flaky test in early runs (migration_simulator/sql_parser_test) was stabilized by simplifying the parser and adding a fixture.

Rollback/runbook: The playbook documents a staged rollback orchestrator that leverages the plan guard's dry-run mode to detect residual drift and the airgap shim's manifest to re-seed missing artifacts.

Steps include: 1) mark tenant for maintenance (installer/scripts/quarantine.sh), 2) snapshot current DB and object storage, 3) run migration simulator to verify revert path, 4) apply rollback release using Helm shim with signed manifest, 5) validate with smoke prompts and metrics.

Security notes: Signed manifests use the existing KMS/HSM integration; the migration simulator never ships snapshots off-cluster unless explicitly exported by an operator.

Known limitations: - Simulator currently supports primary Postgres schemas and a subset of KV transforms; complex stored procedures are not simulated. - Plan guard thresholds require tuning per customer workload.

See upgrade-playbook for mitigation.

add-provenance-anchors-and-version-notary-workflow

Motivation: onboarding workflows currently lack compact, verifiable provenance snippets and a lightweight version notarization step that ties a model upload to deterministic metadata and a stable version token. This PR introduces 'provenance anchors' (compact signed fingerprints derived from model manifest + sample telemetry) and a 'version notary' service that issues short canonical version tokens and generates a succinct release blurb suitable for changelogs and automated release notes.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a provenance anchor generator (tools/anchor_generator.py) that canonicalizes manifest fields, computes a content-hash, and attaches sampled telemetry signatures to improve de-dup and drift detection. 2) Introduces a notary microservice (notary/service.py) that consumes anchors and returns an immutable version token (vtoken) together with a short humanized summary used by release automation. 3) Plumbs anchor metadata into the onboarding pipeline (ingest/worker.py changes) so every successful model intake stores anchor and vtoken in the model index. 4) Adds a changelog helper (scripts/brief_builder.py) that converts vtoken + anchor into a one-paragraph release note draft and a compact manifest excerpt for audits. 5) Tests for anchor stability and notary idempotency (tests/test_anchor.py, tests/test_notary_idempotency.py). 6) CI pipeline updates to run anchor stability matrix on a sample of previously onboarded models.

Design notes: - Anchors are intentionally compact (<= 256 bytes) and include: canonical manifest hash, sampled latency/quantile telemetry fingerprint, and a short provenance salt. Anchors are signed using the existing keystore integration so they can be verified offline. - The vtoken is a short base32 token (8-10 chars) derived from the signed anchor fingerprint; it is intended for human-friendly usage (UIs, changelogs) and is not a replacement for full model versioning semantics. - Notary enforces idempotency: repeated submissions with identical canonical manifest -> same vtoken. Different telemetry samples will be canonicalized into the anchor deterministically. - The changelog helper emits an opinionated short blurb: model alias, vtoken, delta hints (new/changed inputs), and a single-line cost/perf note if telemetry delta > threshold.

We'll rollout to staging for 48 hours, run a smoke ingestion of the nightly model-catalog and verify anchors and vtoken generation. After monitoring (console dashboard widget added), toggle on in production. Backout: disable flag and purge vtoken index writes (safe no-destructive path).

SLO Lease Rebalancer for Soft Regional Handoffs

Background: Regional incidents and maintenance windows frequently force temporary redistribution of SLO responsibility across regions.

Existing failover semantics are abrupt: either route fully to a fallback region or trigger a global throttle, which causes avoidable churn and user-visible latency spikes.

This PR implements a SLO Lease Rebalancer that permits soft, capacity-aware handoffs: regions can donate or acquire SLO leases over a bounded window, with attenuated traffic shifts, circuit-aware backoff, and an emergency reclaim path for correctness.

Design highlights: 1) Lease model: each region holds leases for tenant partitions with a lease_window_ms TTL and an associated capacity_score updated from per-route throughput and node health.

2) Rebalancer algorithm: periodic scoring pass computes donors and receivers and proposes chunked lease transfers sized by capacity_delta and handoff_threshold_pct.

Transfers are staged over windows with exponential backoff on transient failures.

3) Soft resume: receivers apply an attenuated activation that gradually increases weight (0 -> target) so downstream caches and KV warmup reduce cold-start SLO violations.

4) Circuit interplay: when a receiving region has active circuits tripped for a tenant, the transfer is paused and marked for retry; donors maintain temporary sticky leases until a safe handoff can complete.

5) Observability: new lease_migration_success/failure, lease_transfer_duration_ms, and region_capacity_score metrics plus handoff traces.

6) Safety: emergency_force_reclaim shortcut (operator-triggered) for edge cases and a conservatively defaulted handoff_threshold_pct=0.25 to avoid aggressive churn.

Changes made: - runtime/lease_manager.go: core rebalancer, scoring, transfer orchestration, retry/backoff. - runtime/lease_manager_test.go: unit tests covering scoring, chunking, backoff semantics. - routing/handshake.go: handshake extension for staged weight updates and compatibility checks. - observability/metrics/lease_metrics.prom: metric definitions and dashboard hints. - docs/operational/lease-rebalancer.md: runbook, default knobs, and troubleshooting. - deploy/k8s/upgrade-hooks.yaml: prestop hook to drain leases on node removal. - cli/ctl-handoff.sh: convenience operator script to trigger handoffs or force-reclaim. - ops/runbooks/slo-hand-offs.md: incident runbook additions. - examples/handshake-sim.json: simulation scenarios used in testing.

Testing and validation: comprehensive unit coverage added; integration test in perf-canary simulated a cross-region outage and validated a staged handoff with 0.12% SLO breach delta (within target).

Chaos testing included region-level partitioning and node terminations; rebalancer paused transfers and resumed once capacity stabilized.

Performance: small CPU overhead (~3% p99 increase during active rebalances) observed in canary, within SLA.

Rollout plan: canary at 5% traffic in us-west-2 for 2h, monitor lease_migration_success, slo_violation_rate, region_capacity_score and downstream error/latency.

If stable, ramp to 25% for 4h then global.

Auto rollback on >0.5% sustained increase in SLO breaches for 15m or >2s median token latency regression.

Backwards compatibility: no changes to public APIs; all behavior behind runtime feature-flag runtime.slo_lease_rebalancer.enabled=false by default for safe staged rollout.

Operator knobs: lease_window_ms (default 900000), handoff_threshold_pct (default 0.25), max_chunk_size (default 100 partitions), emergency_force_reclaim (manual).

Migration and upgrade notes: ensure dedicated nodes have upgrade-hooks applied to allow graceful lease drain; upgrade order should follow cross-region canary then control plane.

Known limitations and mitigations: in extreme multi-region partition churn the rebalancer defers transfers to avoid oscillation; we log deferred_transfer_* metrics to aid future tuning.

Documentation added and internal runbooks updated.

page-siloing-locality-preserving-evictor-and-spill-attenuation

Context: Our KV cache has increasing fragmentation and frequent small spill writes under mixed workloads (short chat traces + occasional long contexts).

Motivation: reduce tail latency and spill I/O amplification by keeping hot keys co-located in contiguous page 'silos' and by making the evictor prefer locality-preserving demotions.

This PR implements a page siloing allocator, a locality-preserving eviction policy, and a spill attenuation controller that defers and coalesces spill writes when under transient pressure.

Changes are gated behind a runtime flag (kv.page_siloing_enabled) and incremental by default.

Design summary: 1) Page siloing allocator groups allocations into silos by tenant and affinity score computed from recent access fingerprinting.

Silos aim to keep related KV entries on contiguous page ranges to reduce fragmentation and sequentialize spill write patterns.

2) Locality-preserving evictor selects victims not only by recency/heat but also by silo contiguity score so evictions prefer reclaiming whole subranges that yield contiguous free segments.

This substantially reduces micro-fragmentation.

3) Spill attenuation controller monitors spill sink bandwidth and in-flight spill latency; when spikes occur it switches from immediate per-page spill to deferred coalesced-write mode (batching multiple evicted pages into a single larger write, limited by a configurable max_coalesce_bytes).

4) Integration with scheduler: the evictor now exposes a hint to the continuous-batching scheduler so that inflight generation batches avoid pinning tokens to pages that are being reclaimed, reducing KV lookup latency spikes during concurrent eviction.

5) Telemetry and evaluation: new metrics (kv.silo_fill_ratio, kv.eviction_contiguity, kv.spill_coalesce_ratio) and an end-to-end perf test harness that simulates mixed short+long context traffic.

Implementation notes: - New package/runtime files: kv/silo_allocator.{cc,hh}, kv/evictor_locality.cc, kv/spill_attenuator.cc, scheduler/evictor_hints.go - Conservative default config: silo max size = 8MB, coalesce window = 50ms, max_coalesce_bytes = 2MB - Backwards compatible: no public API changes, feature off by default.

Migration path: customers can enable per-tenant via console or feature flags; rollout plan includes dark launches and Canary pool in Dedicated.

Migration path: customers can enable per-tenant via console or feature flags; rollout plan includes dark launches and Canary pool in Dedicated.

Test plan: unit tests for silo placement, fuzz tests for contiguity heuristics, integration perf job in perf-canary (redwood/perf-canary) comparing tail latency and WAN spill traffic.

CI: initial CI run failed on an intermittent scheduler race in continuous batching; fixed by adding a small handshake between evictor and scheduler (evictor_hints now uses a version token to ensure stale hints are ignored).

Outcomes: synthetic perf runs show 18-28% reduction in spill IOPS for mixed workloads and 6-12% tail latency improvement (95th/99th) in our canary environment.

introduce-invocation-compressor-and-slo-smartlink

Context and motivation: customer incident SUP-881 showed long-tail token cost spikes correlated with repeated redundant context blocks across streaming and non-streaming invocations.

This PR introduces an invocation compression middleware (server-side) that detects repeated prefix patterns at the invocation level and compresses the outgoing trace/metric payloads and token-cost annotations for storage and dashboarding.

In parallel, we add a small SLO SmartLink feature that binds compressed invocation fingerprints to SLO incidents so on-call can quickly jump from an SLO violation to representative uncompressed traces for triage.

Design notes: the compressor runs in the observability sidecar and performs a lightweight rolling hash to identify repeated prefix segments and a canonical token-map delta encoding to preserve cost attribution per token.

Compression is lossless for cost attribution metadata and lossy for raw token text (we store a digest to rehydrate only for on-demand debug flows).

The SLO SmartLink stores a compact fingerprint index in the observability metadata service and surfaces a deterministic link in the SLO UI that will trigger a gated rehydration flow and time-bound audit access.

Migration and rollout: feature gated behind 'invocation_compressor' and 'slo_smartlink' feature flags; rollout strategy is staged by tenant percentage with a background backfill job to compress 7 days of recent invocations for opt-in tenants.

Backfill is throttled and can be paused via the console.

Observability impacts: compression reduces storage and query egress for invocation artifacts (estimated ~3x reduction for customers with high prefix reuse).

We add new metrics invocation_compressor.compress_rate, invocation_compressor.rehydrate_latency, and slo_smartlink.link_resolution_time; dashboards included in this PR.

Testing: unit tests for the rolling hash and delta encoding, integration tests exercising end-to-end compression and rehydration, plus a small replaybench scenario with synthetic repeated prompts.

Performance: compressor introduces sub-millisecond overhead on p95 invocation path in production profile; profiling results included in commits.

Rollout notes: start at 5% tenants, monitor compress_rate and rehydrate_latency, escalate abort on >100ms rehydrate p95 or if cost attribution divergence >0.1% on sample prompts.

Related work: follows patterns in ENG-3421 (token-cost attribution) and complements the token-heatmap panels.

starvation-prober-soft-ejector: detect KV-heavy starvation and softly eject to preserve latency SLOs

Motivation: Continuous-batcher occasionally experiences prolonged tail latency during KV-heavy workloads where certain requests pin large KV regions and prevent fair progress for low-KV or stateless requests. Existing admission and fairshare heuristics alleviate this in steady state but do not react fast enough to transient starvation caused by sudden KV-window growth. This PR introduces a starvation prober plus a soft-ejector policy that detects likely starvation windows and gently evicts a small number of KV-hot requests to restore headroom and keep latency SLOs.

What this change does: 1) Adds a lightweight background "starvation prober" that samples queue windows and maintains a short-term KV-load histogram. The prober uses a rolling measurement (3s default) to detect when the effective KV-saturation exceeds a configured threshold relative to lane capacity. 2) Introduces a "soft-ejector" path in the continuous-batcher which, when the prober signals starvation, marks a minimal set of in-flight KV-heavy slots for soft-ejection: they are moved to an expedited eviction path that preserves KV cache warmup where possible (writes back partial KV pins) and optionally hedges to a lower-capacity model variant. 3) Adds a new scheduler hint (kv_evict_score) used by the allocator to prefer ejecting the smallest-effect requests first (by estimated KV pins and remaining tokens). 4) Tuning knobs exposed via config: prober_window_ms, kv_saturation_threshold, soft_eject_max_pct, eject_backoff_ms. 5) New unit and integration tests and an e2e perf benchmark harness that simulates sudden KV pressure spikes.

Why this is safe: soft-ejector does not forcibly kill requests — it moves them to a controlled eviction lane which tries graceful spillback or migration to compatible model variants. The feature is opt-in by default and guarded behind a config flag. Rollout plan is conservative: feature flag off, enable in Canary stage for dedicated pools with 1% traffic, then gradual ramp with telemetry checks for request success rate and KV cache warmth regressions.

Metrics & Observability: new metrics added: runtime.starvation_prober.saturation_ratio, runtime.soft_ejector.ejections_total, runtime.soft_ejector.avg_eject_latency, and tracing tags on ejected requests (eject_reason=starvation_prober). There is a dashboard tile and alert rule suggestion PERF-STARVE-01 (high sustained saturation_ratio >0.85 for >30s).

Related work: follows earlier KV-aware schedulers (ENG-3512) and complements the holdback/reserve features; differs by being transient-probe driven and prioritizing minimal disturbance to overall throughput.

Testing done: unit tests for prober histogram, allocator hint scoring logic; integration tests simulating KV spike then verifying ejections and latency recovery; perf microbenchmark showing 50-70% reduction in 99th percentile tail latency in KV-spike scenario while throughput loss under 3% when soft_eject_max_pct=0.05.

Notes/Docs: added config docs and an ops playbook section explaining when to enable and how to interpret saturation_ratio.

unify-retry-profiles-and-lightweight-stream-helpers-across-sdks

Motivation: SDKs historically contained duplicated retry/backoff and stream ergonomics code that diverged subtly between Python/TypeScript/Go. That made cross-SDK behavior inconsistent (different default jitter, different max_retry windows) and increased maintenance burden. This PR extracts a transport-agnostic RetryProfile and introduces a tiny, consistent set of lightweight stream helpers for each SDK so app code can be ported with fewer surface changes.

What this PR does (high level):
- Introduce a core RetryProfile concept and backoff parameter mapping used by all SDKs (max_attempts, initial_backoff_ms, max_backoff_ms, jitter_mode, hedged_retries).
- Replace ad-hoc retry logic in each SDK with small adapters that map RetryProfile -> transport specific retry strategies.
- Add ergonomic streaming helpers: Python async generator wrapper (stream.iter_lines_safe), TS async iterable shim (stream.consumeSafe), Go StreamHandle interface + convenience ReadPump.
- Add cross-SDK unit/compat tests that assert parity on default retry timeline for common scenarios (auth 401 then refresh, transient 429, slow downstream).
- Documentation: migration guide and explicit examples for moving from the legacy per-SDK backoff flags to the unified RetryProfile.
- Version bumps: python sdk -> 0.12.0, typescript sdk -> 1.27.0, go sdk -> 1.8.0.

Why transport-agnostic RetryProfile: Teams run heterogeneous stacks (frontend TS, backend Python, microservice in Go). Previously, moving a workload between services required tuning three different knobs. The RetryProfile is a single well-documented primitive that can be serialized as JSON, stored in config, and applied consistently across languages.

Migration notes:
- If you set per-SDK backoff env flags (RETRY_INITIAL_MS, RETRY_MAX_MS, RETRY_ATTEMPTS), they will continue to be read but are deprecated — migrate to a RetryProfile config shipped to your service.
- Streaming helper names changed: start_stream -> open_stream is preserved at the transport level but helper names for safe iteration are new (see examples in docs/sdk/migration/retry-profile.md).

Scope and risk: The change is primarily additive (new adapters + helpers) but rewires retry decision points in each SDK. We validated with end-to-end test harness and Canary run against staging traffic for 48h.

improve-streaming-backpressure-kernel-pacing-and-flush-cadence

Motivation: production streaming customers saw 95th/99th token latency spikes when model sequence interleaving and kernel dispatch jitter aligned under high concurrency.

Root causes identified: the token emission loop was flushing per-request too aggressively, kernel selection introduced micro-scheduling stalls on heterogenous sequences, and continuous-batching queues lacked a backpressure signal tied to active KV cache memory pressure.

This PR addresses these by (1) introducing an adaptive flush cadence that groups sub-token flushes into a short window to amortize syscalls and network writes while preserving low tail latency for first tokens, (2) adding a soft backpressure token to the continuous-batcher that temporarily reduces per-request batching depth when KV cache hit-rate drops or memory pressure rises, (3) pacing kernel dispatch for mixed sequence lengths via a simple cost-estimator in the kernel selector to avoid dispatching long-seq kernels immediately ahead of short-seq work, and (4) minor refactors to the token loop to separate emission, checkpointing, and stall-detection logic.

Implementation summary: streamer.cpp now tracks per-stream last-flush timestamp and an adaptive_window_ms computed from recent per-token latency percentiles; a new flush_coalescer module consolidates writes within the window. continuous_batcher adds a backpressure_count that increments when kv_cache_manager reports degraded hit_rate or memory_watermark>0.8; when backpressure_count>threshold, the batcher lowers max_batch_size and exposes a diagnostics metric. kernel_selector computes a normalized cost metric (compute_tokens*cost_factor + io_penalty) and delays high-cost kernels by small randomized jitter to reduce head-of-line blocking.

Observability: added metrics streaming.flush_coalesce_ratio, batcher.backpressure_level, kernel.pacing_delay and tagged spans for flush-window boundary events.

Tests and benchmarks: synthetic microbenchmarks show 95th token latency reduction of 18-32% across r4 and a100 instances for mixed-long/short workloads, and overall token throughput maintained within 2% of baseline.

Safety and rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.streaming.adaptive_flush=true and batcher backpressure disabled by default.

Rollout plan: enable in canary for 10% of traffic for 48h, monitor streaming.flush_coalesce_ratio and tail-token SLOs and KV cache hit_rate; automatic rollback if 95th latency regresses >5%.

Streamlined credential fallback and multi-SDK pullstream ergonomics

Motivation: multiple SDK teams and downstream apps reported subtle mismatch in credential handoff semantics between Python/TS/Go pull-stream implementations and a confusing fallback surface that made token rotation fragile. This PR consolidates the credential fallback strategy into a small composable "CredFallbackChain" and rationalizes the pullstream iterator shape across SDKs so that caller ergonomics and retry semantics are consistent.

Summary of changes (single-pass continuous description): Implement CredFallbackChain abstraction with three pluggable providers (env -> cached refresh -> delegated callback). Add lightweight CredLease helper that exposes expires_at and refresh_if_needed hooks. Replace legacy token swap hooks in Python/TS/Go SDKs with a single adapter layer that translates chain outcomes into the language-specific session objects. Introduce PullStream.v2 ergonomics: a single async iterator pattern that yields chunk envelopes and exposes a .resume() hook for resumable streams; ensure backpressure is preserved for TS and Go via the same resume semantics. Unify retry profile defaults across SDKs: 3 fast-retries for handshake, exponential backoff for token refresh, idempotent request hints for streaming resumes. Add parity test harnesses that exercise cross-language replay of a recorded streaming session to validate token-rotation timing, resume correctness, and finalization semantics. Bump SDK versions: python 0.42.1 -> 0.43.0, typescript 2.1.0 -> 2.2.0, go 0.9.4 -> 0.10.0.

dsid_02cf33ea86a547dea1126521e9886307__p.text:
soft fallback mapper for legacy tool envelopes and streaming stability

Summary: Adds a non-destructive backward-compatibility layer that maps legacy v1 'tool envelopes' and mixed-mode streaming events into the current structured tool-calling shape. This is a runtime-level, opt-out behavior controlled by a lightweight request header (X-RW-Compat: legacy=1) and a server-side fallback profile. Motivation: We continue to see client integrations that emit the older tool/function envelope format and interleave streaming 'event' fragments that do not align with the v2 structured tool-call and streaming framing. These cause either broken tool invocation or stream mangling for customers who cannot upgrade immediately. This PR provides a safety net so clients can continue to operate while we deprecate v1 on a scheduled timeline.

What this change does (single-line sections concatenated into this description): - Adds a LegacyEnvelopeMapper in the API gateway that coalesces fragmented streaming events into a canonical tool-call request object when the compat header is present. - Introduces X-RW-Compat header handling and a short-lived server-side flag for rollout (defaults disabled). - Adds unit and integration tests that simulate partial streaming frames, nested tool payloads, and mixed text-with-tool streams. - Exposes a per-tenant opt-in via Console feature flag and adds telemetry to track how often mappings are used and whether coercion dropped any fields. - Adds a best-effort deterministic fallback for ambiguous payloads: the mapper will prefer tool metadata in this order: explicit tool_name > envelope.tool > legacy_inferred_name.

Implementation notes and constraints: - The fallback is intentionally conservative: fields are not removed; ambiguous sub-fields are placed under a legacy_metadata map on the coerced payload so v2 handlers can log and surface them without losing data. - Mapper runs early in the request handling pipeline to preserve KV cache keys and batching behavior. - This PR does not change the public schema contract unless the compat header is supplied.

Tests and CI: - Commits include a new suite that replays recorded incident streams (replay fixtures) where older clients sent 3-part event envelopes; these fixtures were captured from a postmortem trace and scrubbed. - CI matrix covers gateway unit tests, end-to-end gateway->runtime smoke, and SDK regression checks. - Initial CI run failed on a flaky streaming test; flake fixed with a deterministic buffering tweak.

Commits (high-level): - feat(gateway): add legacy envelope mapper and header parsing - test(gateway): add replay fixtures and streaming integration tests - feat(console): tenant opt-in flag and telemetry hooks - fix(tests): deterministic buffer improvement to stabilize CI - docs: add compatibility guide and scheduled deprecation note

Files changed (high level): - gateway/compat/LegacyEnvelopeMapper.go (core mapping logic and heuristics) - gateway/handlers/stream_decoder.go (stream coalescing, small buffering change) - runtime/handler/tool_invoker.go (adds legacy_metadata passthrough) - console/flags/compat_flags.go (tenant opt-in surface) - telemetry/mappers/compat_telemetry.go (usage counters and histograms) - test/fixtures/legacy_stream_replays/ (three JSONL fixtures) - docs/compatibility/legacy-to-structured.md (how to opt in/opt out and examples)

Review conversation highlights (excerpted and paraphrased into a single string): - Oliver Park: "Nice conservative approach. Question: what happens to token-level billing attribution when we coalesce fragments?" Author reply: "We preserve token counts and annotate the coerced payload; billing code reads token totals from the annotated envelope unchanged." - Sana Iqbal: "Ensure mapper is O(1) memory for tiny fragments; we don't want it to buffer entire large streams." Author reply: "Mapper bounds to max 8KB aggregation window, then emits partial-coercion with legacy_metadata and a telemetry counter for truncated envelopes." - Diego Morales requested an additional integration test for tool-call failure paths; author added it in second commit. introduce-resilient-dedicated-throttle-controller-and-percentile-throughput-reporter

Adds a DedicatedThrottleController to smooth burst allocations and a PercentileThroughputReporter metric for SLA visibility.

Backwards compatible; config defaults preserve existing behavior.

Operators should review new helm values documented in the release notes.

Motivation: Dedicated capacity customers need predictable throughput guarantees even during fleet-wide transient surges and node churn.

Existing burst allocation logic can over-commit short-lived warm pools and create noisy percentile signals in observability.

This PR introduces a DedicatedThrottleController, a small control-plane component that enforces soft per-tenant token smoothing, speculative backfill limits, and a drift-correction heuristic that prevents slow leak/accumulate behaviors when telemetry is sparse.

The controller is configurable by tenant-level policy and integrated with the existing fleet headroom allocator so it can provide graceful degradation rather than hard rejects.

We also add a PercentileThroughputReporter that computes 50/90/99 throughput percentiles for each tenant over sliding windows and emits both summary and raw-sample metrics for downstream reporting and SLO evaluation.

Design highlights: 1) Token smoothing: uses a leaky-bucket style accumulator with a two-timescale smoothing (fast window for immediate burst allowance, slow window for baseline throughput) and an adjustable recovery factor to support graceful reduction after sustained high load.

2) Speculative backfill limiter: allows short-lived allocation from ephemeral warmlets but caps effective concurrency headroom per-tenant so large tenants cannot monopolize burst slots during cluster-wide surges.

3) Drift-correction heuristic: when the reporter detects steady mismatch between requested capacity and observed completions, the controller applies conservative calibration to the smoothing parameters to avoid runaway optimistic allocations.

4) Telemetry: the PercentileThroughputReporter emits per-tenant throughput percentiles (p50/p90/p99 tokens/sec), a burst-utilization ratio, and a 'smoothed_headroom' gauge used by autoscaler advisors.

5) Compatibility: new helm values default to disabled for clusters with custom schedulers; enabling requires setting dedicated.throttleController.enabled=true.

5) Compatibility: new helm values default to disabled for clusters with custom schedulers; enabling requires setting dedicated.throttleController.enabled=true.

Implementation notes: changes span controller code (pkg/controllers/dedicated_throttle.go), allocator integrations (pkg/allocator/headroom_adapter.go), telemetry (pkg/telemetry/percentile_reporter.go), a small operator CRD addition (deploy/crds/dedicatedpolicy.yaml), unit and e2e tests (pkg/controllers/*_test.go, test/e2e/dedicated_throttle_test.go), and chart values (charts/dedicated/values.yaml).

Tests: added deterministic unit tests for smoothing math, three e2e scenarios that simulate short microbursts, sustained high load, and telemetry sparsity, plus a load harness run that asserts no regressions in 95th percentile latency.

Observability: dashboards updated (observability/dashboards/dedicated_throttle.json) and a short runbook entry included (docs/ops/dedicated_throttle_runbook.md).

Rollout plan: staged rollout behind the helm flag with canary percentage by tenant label; operator tooling will surface the new percentile metrics and suggestion engine will recommend knob values based on historical load.

Backwards compatibility: controllers default to no-op if DedicatedPolicy CRD not present and helm flag is off.

Related work: builds on ENG-1427 (headroom allocator refactor), leverages some heuristics from ENG-1683 (burst bank smoothing).

Cohort-traceback fanout conductor with interruptible rollback and explainable recovery

Summary: Introduces the 'Cohort Traceback Fanout Conductor' (CTFC), a rollout controller that prioritizes session-coherent cohorts for canary/A-B promotions, supports interruptible rollbacks mid-fanout, and exposes an explainable rollback oracle that surfaces the minimal contributing signals when a promote fails.

Motivation: Recent incidents showed large blast radii when promotions ignored session affinity and when rollbacks were binary and opaque. CTFC reduces user-visible regressions by ensuring fans are constrained to cohort boundaries, enabling on-the-fly interruption, and providing triageable telemetry to SREs and PMs.

- Explainable rollback oracle: a modular evaluator that runs a compact counterfactual smoke replay on recent samples and returns ranked signal contributions.
- Safety budget integration: honor existing rollout budget tokens and expose a credit refund when early-interrupts avoid downstream degradation.
- Dry-run mode: a CLI flag and API path that runs validation without committing traffic.
- Tests: e2e smoke harness that replays recorded traffic and unit tests for oracle scorer.

throughput-sla-convergence-orchestrator-and-util-snapshotter

Motivation: Dedicated capacity currently relies on static commitments or reactive scaling which causes oscillation between over-provision and underutilization. This PR introduces a Convergence Orchestrator that gradually aligns tenant reservations to sustained observed throughput while preserving short-duration burst headroom via a multiplexer guard. It also adds a Utilization Snapshotter that emits compact occupancy deltas used by the orchestrator and the consoles/alerts.

Summary of changes: 
- Convergence Orchestrator: controller that computes a target reservation fraction based on exponentially-weighted sustained throughput, a conservative safety multiplier, and a configurable hysteresis window. Includes safeguards to avoid starvation when traffic patterns shift abruptly.
- Multiplexer Guard: logic that preserves a small burst allowance above the converged reservation so latency-sensitive requests get occasional headroom without impacting long-term guarantees.
- Utilization Snapshotter: lightweight service that samples per-tenant occupancy and tokenized throughput every 30s, emits compact delta metrics and a rolling 5-min histogram. Designed for low overhead and export to both Prometheus and the internal telemetry pipeline.
- Config and runtime flags: new config fields under dedicated.autoscale: convergence_window_sec, safety_multiplier, burst_multiplier, snapshot_interval_sec, snapshot_histogram_buckets. Default values chosen to be conservative.
- Telemetry and dashboards: new metrics (tenant_reservation_target, tenant_snapshot_util_p50/p90/p99, tenant_burst_allowed) and a dashboard tile.
- Tests and e2e: unit tests for convergence math, integration harness to validate no-regression in steady throughput, and a small canary job used during rollout.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-1984)
- [x] Unit tests added for convergence math and snapshot aggregation
- [x] Integration test validating no oscillation on synthetic peaky workloads
- [x] Telemetry and dashboard added
- [x] Feature-gated rollout with canary enabled

Design notes and safety: 
The orchestrator uses an EWMA over a 5m window (configurable) to derive a sustained throughput estimate. The target reservation is sustained_throughput * safety_multiplier. The burst allowance is burst_multiplier * sqrt(target_reservation) (heuristic chosen to scale sub-linearly with reservation) and strictly capped by a global per-pool burst budget. All changes are gated behind dedicated.flags.enable_sla_convergence. If the orchestrator is disabled, existing reservation logic is unchanged.

Rollout plan: 
1) Merge feature-flag guarded code to main behind disabled-by-default flag.
2) Enable in Canary fleet for 48 hours, monitor tenant_reservation_target drift and tenant_snapshot_util_p90.
3) Gradually enable on 10% of Dedicated fleets for 72 hours, validate no increased latency tail.
4) Ramp to 100% with monitoring and progressive rollback window.

Testing performed: 
- Unit: convergence math edge cases (zero traffic, sudden spike, gradual ramp).
- Integration: two-week synthetic run comparing static reservations vs orchestrator in a dedicated cluster; observed 12% reduction in average spare capacity with <1% increase in 99th latency.
- Load: canary run with 200 tenants, random sine-wave traffic; orchestrator converged within configured window and respected burst budget.

Introduce lightweight CI emulator and shared cache protocol to speed local dev feedback

Summary: This PR introduces a small cross-platform CI emulator (ci-emu) and a tiny shared cache protocol that together let engineers run a faithful, fast subset of our GitHub Actions pipelines locally or in ephemeral CI.

Motivation: developers today wait multiple minutes for CI feedback from full workflows.

The emulator reproduces job ordering, environment variable injection, matrix selection pruning, and artifact/cache lookup semantics but runs tasks locally (or in a remote dev runner) with a fraction of the overhead.

The cache protocol is intentionally minimal (versioned headers + content-addressed blobs) to allow safe sharing between ephemeral runners and local dev without requiring a centralized service.

Goals: 1) reduce round-trip time for lint/test/fast-integration by ~3-5x for most changes, 2) shrink the need to run full matrix jobs during early iteration, 3) keep production release pipelines untouched and gated.

What changed (high level): - tools/ci/ci-emu/ : new Go-based emulator binary and small config loader (cli + library) - infra/ci/cache-protocol.md : spec for the cache protocol (HTTP headers, blob layout, simple attestation) - .github/workflows/ci-lite.yml : new lightweight workflow that calls the emulator in remote runner mode for ephemeral CI - scripts/ci/patch-workflow.sh : helper to run emulated subsets locally with the same env as Actions - ci/pinning/actions-versions.json : added pins for a couple of actions used by the emulator to reduce runtime surprises - docs/dev/ci-emulator.md : onboarding and troubleshooting guide Design notes: - ci-emu intentionally executes user-defined commands (make test, ./scripts/run-lint) in separate processes and captures stdout/stderr with timestamps so output ordering mirrors Actions logs. - The cache protocol uses a small JSON header with schema v1 and a content-addressed blob (sha256).

Servers can implement it behind any transport; our implementation includes a tiny in-repo file-backed store for dev and a simple ephemeral s3-compatible example for CI. - Security: the emulator does not attempt to expose secrets; it only replays env vars provided by workflows.

We added a whitelist for envs and a --allow-secrets flag for opt-in scenarios. - Non-goal: this change is not a full replacement for Actions; production release, E2E, and long-running matrix jobs still use the existing workflows.

Key rotation procedure + audit evidence checklist (KMS/Private)

Summary: Adds customer/operator-facing documentation for key rotation in Redwood Private/Dedicated contexts, plus an audit-friendly evidence checklist that maps cleanly to common SOC2/ISO narratives. This PR is intended to reduce back-and-forth during enterprise security reviews by making our rotation steps and evidence artifacts explicit and repeatable.

Context / why: Regulated customers (and prospects) are asking for (a) a clear rotation procedure (including rollback criteria) and (b) the exact evidence they can expect to produce/receive (who approved, what changed, when it happened, what logs prove it). This doc set aligns with the ongoing KMS hardening effort and the rotation strategy in ADR-008.

What’s included: 1) New page: “Key rotation procedure (KMS envelope encryption)” covering prerequisites, roles/responsibilities (Customer vs Redwood), staged rollout, dual-read window, cutover, verification, and rollback. 2) New page: “Rotation evidence checklist” that can be used as a runbook attachment and as audit evidence. Includes templates for a rotation log entry, required screenshots/exports, and pointers to audit log event types. 3) Updates to navigation + cross-links from the Private KMS Operator Guide and Security FAQ sections to reduce discoverability issues.

Audience: Private operators, SRE/on-call, Security/GRC reviewers, Sales/SE support during enterprise security reviews.

introduce-temporal-tilt-detector-and-daypart-smoothing-dashboard

Motivation: transient daypart and seasonal patterns were generating noisy token-cost alerts and paging on short-lived shifts.

This PR implements a lightweight 'Temporal Tilt Detector' that combines a daypart-aware baseline (hour-of-day/week-of-day bucketing), an EWMA trend baseline, and a seasonal-trend decomposition stage to produce a bounded tilt_score per route/tenant.

The tilt_score is emitted as a low-cardinality metric and as a span tag to enable correlated traces for root-cause.

Changes include: (1) new telemetry exporter fields (tilt_score, daypart, rolling_baseline) and bounded aggregation keys; (2) trace enrichment for tilt tagging; (3) a Grafana dashboard "Daypart Tilt & Cost Smoothing" with panels for tilt, smoothed token-cost, raw vs baseline, per-tenant drift heatmap and suggested mitigation actions; (4) updated alert rules that use dampening (15m suppression window for small tilts) and hysteresis to avoid flapping; (5) incident-bot integration to defer low-severity pages automatically when tilt is transient and non-regressive; (6) unit + integration tests and a micro-benchmark to validate detector latency on median payloads.

Design notes: to control cardinality we bucket daypart into 6 coarse zones and restrict tilt emission to aggregation keys {route, model_family, tenant_tier} by default with an opt-in fine-grained label.

We include a sampling guard for high-cardinality tenants and aggregate sketches for rollups.

See docs link: RFC https://linear.app/redwood/ENG-1987 for algorithm rationale.

Compact defaults matrix and fallback planner for cost-aware inference

Motivation: many customers hit higher-than-expected unit costs because sensible batching, cache, and quantization defaults are either too aggressive for small tail workloads or too conservative for high-throughput tenants.

This PR introduces a compact defaults matrix generator plus a fallback planner that simplifies autopilot behavior for Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments and gives ops explicit, auditable rules for graceful degradation.

Key changes: 1) defaults matrix builder that consumes workload sketches (p95 latency, seq length distribution, qps buckets) and emits a small set of presets (batch_size, prefill_budget, kv_cache_ttl, quant_profile) tuned by cost-latency tradeoffs; 2) fallback planner that maps SLOs and capacity tiers to ordered fallback strategies (scale, model-variant, quant-fallback, regional-failover) and exposes a deterministic evaluation function for rollouts; 3) telemetry and unit-econ calibration hooks (metrics + synthetic-sample harness) so we can measure expected unit cost delta before enabling a profile; 4) CLI and Console surface to preview and apply suggested defaults; 5) docs and canary rollout plan.

Checklist: implements unit tests and integration smoke tests; adds example workload sketches; includes rollout playbook and rollback steps; updates docs.

Rollout plan: staged canary on 10% of new Hosted signups -> 25% -> 100% across regions with observability gating on unit_econ_regression and latency_violation alerts.

Related work: ENG-4321 (cost defaults), ENG-4390 (fallback routing policies), SUP-1209 (customer support case patterns).

Notable limitations: profiler relies on representative replay traces; aggressive quant profiles are gated by quality regression monitors.

Shadow traffic: telemetry events + ingestion hooks (v1)

Context: Shadow traffic routing (ENG-5402) mirrors a sampled subset of prod requests to one or more shadow targets. To compute quality deltas (and to debug routing/scoring lag) we need a low-cardinality, privacy-aware set of telemetry events that (a) links the control and shadow inference outcomes, (b) can be ingested reliably in Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and (c) provides enough dimensions to slice by route/model/region without exploding metrics cardinality.

This PR introduces shadow traffic telemetry events and wires them into the ingestion pipeline (Kafka -> ingest -> warehouse tables) with initial dashboard stubs for internal dogfood.

What’s included: (1) New event schemas: shadow_pair_created (emitted when the mirror is scheduled), shadow_inference_completed (shadow target returned or timed out), and shadow_scoring_status (async scoring queued/completed/failed). Each event includes a stable shadow_pair_id and request_fingerprint (HMAC), plus required dimensions: tenant_id (hashed), route_id (low-card), control_model_id, shadow_target_id, deployment_mode, region, outcome, and timing fields. (2) Cardinality controls: disallow freeform tags in shadow telemetry, bucket user_agent, truncate prompt_length/response_length into fixed buckets, and explicitly drop prompt_id / conversation_id at emit-time. Route-level and model-level dimensions are included; anything higher-card must be attached via example sampling endpoints later (out of scope). (3) Ingestion pipeline hooks: adds validators/normalizers for the new events, forwards them through the existing ingest service, and creates the initial storage tables shadow_pairs_v1 and shadow_scoring_v1 (partitioned by day, clustered by tenant_hash + route_id). (4) Initial dashboards stubs: adds basic Grafana JSON stubs for shadow throughput, shadow target error rate, and scoring lag; these are intentionally minimal and will be expanded in observability-pack PR-391.

PII / data handling: This PR does not store raw prompts/responses. request_fingerprint is computed using an HMAC keyed per environment (see config), and tenant_id is hashed before leaving the data plane. Any headers included are allowlisted (content-type, accept, x-redwood-route) and explicitly exclude auth/cookie-like fields.

Testing: Unit tests for schema validation and normalization, golden tests for event-to-table mapping, and an end-to-end ingest test that emits a synthetic shadow_pair_created + shadow_inference_completed and asserts the warehouse row shape. Load testing / overhead benchmarking is tracked in ENG-5412.

Rollout plan: gated behind feature flag shadow_telemetry_v1 (default off). Dogfood tenants can enable via internal config. Fail-open: telemetry emission failures do not impact request path; ingestion lag only affects dashboards/metrics.

Follow-ups: (a) scoring payload references once redaction pipeline lands (ENG-5411), (b) additional aggregation views for confidence intervals, (c) tighten SLO alert thresholds once we have baseline dogfood data.

prioritized-runbook-queue-with-decay-and-responder-snooze

Motivation: On-call queues accumulate runbooks and playbooks with varying usefulness over time.

When multiple responders act concurrently, noisy low-value runbooks surface first and important but less-frequent playbooks are delayed.

This change introduces a prioritized runbook queue that ranks candidate runbooks by a decaying relevance score, supports per-responder snooze windows, and exposes metrics and config for safe rollout.\n\nWhat this PR does: 1) Implements a RunbookScorer service that computes a composite score from incident signal (severity, error-class frequency), recent successful mitigations, runbook age, and team-defined priority tags.

Scores decay over time using an exponential half-life configurable per team.

2) Adds a prioritized queue layer to the incident-bot dispatcher that returns top-N runbooks for a responder instead of FIFO.

3) Adds responder-level snooze: when a responder marks a runbook as "snoozed" it is hidden for that user for a configurable backoff (defaults: 30m/2h/24h tiers).

4) Safe requeueing: runbooks that are requeued by agents get a temporary suppression boost if they repeatedly trigger for the same incident to avoid flapping.

5) Observability: Prometheus metrics (runbook_queue_size, avg_top_score, snooze_events_total, rescore_latency_seconds) and an OpenTelemetry trace span around scoring and dispatch.

6) Admin UI flags and feature-gates for gradual rollout (global, team-level, and user opt-out).\n\nChecklist: - [x] Core scorer implementation and unit tests - [x] Prioritized queue integration and E2E smoke test against local emulated dispatcher - [x] Responder snooze UI endpoint + backend handling - [x] Metrics and tracing hooks - [x] Linear links and config knobs - [x] Feature gate + rollout plan - [x] Docs PR (linked)\n\nRollout plan: Stage 1 (canary): enable for internal oncall with runbook sampling, observe top-score distribution and alert on sudden queue-length regressions.

Stage 2: enable team-by-team via console flag for teams that opt-in.

Stage 2: enable team-by-team via console flag for teams that opt-in.

Stage 3: wide rollout with 7-day monitoring window and automatic rollback on SLO regressions.\n\nCompatibility and fallback: If RunbookScorer fails or times out (>=250ms default), dispatcher reverts to FIFO and emits a metric runbook_score_failures_total.

Feature is entirely opt-in via flags.\n\nNotes: Tuning guidance included in the README.
